Personal discipline is essential to sustained learning, but schools and colleges can strongly affect whether students develop it. I partly disagree that learning is primarily an individual matter beyond institutional motivation.

A student may be interested in chemistry yet struggle to work consistently. A teacher who sets manageable experiments, gives prompt feedback, and shows how each lesson builds toward a question can help the student form habits of study. The work remains the student's own, but the environment makes effort more purposeful. A poorly organized course could make the same student feel that effort yields little progress.

Discipline also matters when external encouragement ends. A university student who wants to master a language must practice between classes and continue after graduation. No instructor can supply that effort by praise alone. Moreover, rewards such as grades can prompt short-term compliance without producing curiosity or resilience.

Institutions should therefore teach students how to plan, recover from mistakes, and seek help while making the subject worth learning. Students must accept responsibility for practicing these habits. The claim is right to reject the fantasy that a school can learn on a student's behalf. It is wrong if it excuses schools from creating the conditions in which motivation and discipline can grow together.

topic: Scientists and other researchers should focus their research on areas that are likely to benefit the greatest number of people.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the recommendation and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, describe specific circumstances in which adopting the recommendation would or would not be advantageous and explain how these examples shape your position.
essay:
Research that benefits many people deserves substantial support, but scientists should not focus exclusively on projects with the largest foreseeable audience. I partly disagree with the recommendation because the value and eventual reach of a discovery can be difficult to predict.

Studying an affordable water-treatment method could improve health for millions. Public agencies should consider that likely benefit when allocating scarce funds. A research system indifferent to urgent needs would fail people who cannot wait for a distant breakthrough. The potential scale of benefit is a legitimate priority.

Yet a project involving a rare disease may matter enormously to a small group. Work on its underlying mechanism can also illuminate more common conditions. Similarly, basic research in mathematics or physics may have no identifiable audience at first, then support technologies used broadly decades later. If funding depends only on an immediate estimate of beneficiaries, such work may never begin.

Risk and ethics also matter. A project promised to benefit millions cannot automatically justify exposing participants to unreasonable danger. Research agencies should weigh scientific merit, need, feasibility, uncertainty, and distribution of benefits rather than maximize one number.

A balanced portfolio can finance urgent public-health work, neglected communities, and open-ended inquiry. The recommendation is useful as a reminder that science serves people, but it becomes counterproductive when “greatest number” is treated as a formula that excludes minority needs and unpredictable discovery.

topic: Politicians should pursue common ground and reasonable consensus rather than elusive ideals.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the recommendation and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, describe specific circumstances in which adopting the recommendation would or would not be advantageous and explain how these examples shape your position.
essay:
Political ideals give leaders a direction, while consensus can turn a direction into durable policy. I mostly agree that politicians should pursue common ground rather than insist on an elusive perfect outcome, provided compromise does not surrender basic rights.

Imagine a legislature debating cleaner energy. Some members want an immediate ban on all fossil fuels; others fear that workers and low-income households will bear the costs. A policy that phases in standards while funding retraining and cheaper alternatives may achieve real emissions reductions. Waiting for unanimous support for a flawless plan could leave pollution unchanged.

Compromise has limits. A majority might offer a deal that preserves discriminatory voting rules in exchange for progress elsewhere. A politician should not call that reasonable merely because several powerful groups agree. Some principles define who can participate in the negotiation at all. Leaders need to explain those boundaries openly and seek other ways to advance a just policy.

Consensus is also valuable when people must live with a decision after an election. Hearing objections can reveal practical flaws and build the trust needed for implementation. But a politician who continually dilutes a proposal to avoid criticism may accomplish little. The standard should be whether a compromise preserves the central purpose while addressing legitimate concerns.

Ideals and common ground are not enemies. The strongest leaders use principles to identify the destination and negotiation to make attainable progress toward it. They should refuse unjust deals, but they should not confuse refusing any imperfect deal with fidelity to an ideal.

topic: People should undertake risky action only after they have carefully considered its consequences.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the recommendation and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, describe specific circumstances in which adopting the recommendation would or would not be advantageous and explain how these examples shape your position.
essay:
Risky action should generally follow careful consideration of its consequences. I agree with the recommendation, although the amount of deliberation must reflect how much time is available and how serious the risk is.

An entrepreneur considering a loan to open a business should estimate demand, examine repayment terms, and ask what would happen if revenue arrives slowly. The analysis cannot guarantee success, but it can prevent an avoidable collapse and suggest a smaller pilot project. Courage is more useful when paired with an understanding of what might go wrong.

Some decisions cannot wait for exhaustive research. If a bystander sees a person drowning, calling emergency services and using available rescue equipment may be better than spending several minutes calculating every outcome. Training in advance can make quick action safer. Careful consideration in such a case may mean following a practiced rule and avoiding a rescue attempt that would create a second victim.

There is also a cost to endless deliberation. A student who postpones every challenging application until success is certain may lose opportunities. After identifying plausible benefits and harms, people sometimes must decide under uncertainty and learn from the result.

The recommendation is strongest when risk falls on others who have not consented, or when harm could be irreversible. It is weaker as a demand for perfect foresight before any experiment. Thoughtful action means considering consequences seriously, using safeguards, and recognizing when further analysis would add little.

topic: Leaders are created by the demands that are placed on them.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the statement and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the statement might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
essay:
Demanding circumstances can bring leadership into view, but they do not create it from nothing. I partly agree with the statement: challenges can develop and reveal qualities that ordinary routines leave untested, while preparation and support shape how a person responds.

During a flood, a neighborhood resident might coordinate shelter, food, and information even though she holds no office. The emergency gives her a reason to act and others a reason to follow. She may learn to delegate and make decisions under pressure. In that sense the demand helps create a leader, rather than merely selecting one already recognized.

Yet two people facing the same crisis may respond differently. Someone who has practiced organizing community events or listening to disagreements is better equipped to coordinate help. Resources matter too: an effective response may depend on volunteers, trusted institutions, and reliable information. It would be unfair to praise one person as naturally heroic while ignoring the network that made action possible.

Leadership also develops in less dramatic settings. A teacher who regularly builds a cooperative classroom or a manager who prepares colleagues to make decisions has been leading before a crisis arrives. Their work may prevent a difficult situation from becoming an emergency at all.

The statement usefully challenges the idea that leaders are born with a fixed title or trait. Demands provide occasions for people to grow into responsibility. But lasting leadership comes from the interaction of circumstance, preparation, judgment, and the willingness of others to work together.

topic: There is little justification for society to make extraordinary efforts — especially at a great cost in money and jobs — to save endangered animal or plant species.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the statement and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the statement might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
essay:
Conservation can be expensive, but its value is not captured by the immediate cost in jobs or public money. I disagree that extraordinary efforts to save endangered species have little justification. The right decision depends on ecological consequences, feasibility, and who bears the burden.

If a wetland species helps sustain an ecosystem that filters drinking water and supports fisheries, its loss may impose costs far beyond the conservation budget. Protecting habitat can benefit both the species and nearby communities. In that case, calling preservation an expense while ignoring the services the ecosystem provides is incomplete accounting.

Yet conservation is not automatically justified at any price. A plan that closes a major employer overnight without offering workers alternatives may cause severe harm. Officials should consider habitat restoration, changes in industrial practices, compensation, and retraining before imposing such a burden. Some projects may have little chance of saving the species despite enormous cost, in which case other conservation priorities may be more responsible.

Even where the practical benefits are uncertain, people may reasonably believe that driving a unique species to extinction is an irreversible loss. Human responsibility for the threat strengthens the obligation to act. The challenge is to design a response that does not ask vulnerable communities to carry all the costs.

Extraordinary efforts require extraordinary justification, but that justification can exist. A careful comparison of long-term ecological value, likelihood of success, and human costs is more useful than a blanket dismissal of endangered species.

topic: The human mind will always be superior to machines because machines are only tools of human minds.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the statement and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the statement might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
essay:
Machines perform tasks that once seemed to require uniquely human intelligence. I therefore disagree with the claim that the human mind will always be superior simply because machines are its tools. Their human origin does not determine their relative ability at every task.

A calculator is designed by people yet performs lengthy arithmetic faster and more reliably than its inventor. A computer can search millions of possible patterns in medical images and flag cases a busy clinician might miss. These examples do not show that a machine understands a patient's fear or should make a diagnosis without oversight. They do show that being a tool is compatible with surpassing human performance in a particular domain.

The statement may mean that humans are superior in choosing goals and taking moral responsibility. At present, a hospital must decide what risks are acceptable and who is accountable when an automated system fails. Those are social judgments, not merely computations. But “always” is a prediction about future capabilities that the fact of human design cannot prove.

Tools can also change the abilities of their users. A scientist working with a powerful model may solve a problem neither the scientist nor the model would solve as effectively alone. The useful comparison is often among systems of people and machines rather than a contest between isolated minds.

We should assess each technology by evidence of what it can do, where it fails, and who governs its use. Human judgment remains indispensable in many decisions, but the categorical claim of permanent superiority mistakes the origin of a machine for a limit on its performance.

topic: People who are the most deeply committed to an idea or policy are also the most critical of it.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the statement and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the statement might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
essay:
Deep commitment sometimes makes people attentive to every weakness in an idea they cherish. Yet it can also make criticism feel like a threat. I disagree that the most committed supporters are generally the most critical, although the strongest forms of commitment can include honest self-examination.

A scientist who has spent years developing a theory may run rigorous tests because she wants the theory to explain the world accurately. If a result contradicts her prediction, acknowledging it can improve the work. Her commitment is to discovery as much as to a particular conclusion. A political organizer may likewise criticize a campaign's tactics because ineffective or unfair methods would harm the cause.

Other committed people react differently. A leader whose identity and career depend on a policy may dismiss evidence that it is failing. Loyal colleagues may avoid raising objections for fear of weakening the group. The deeper their attachment to the specific position, the harder it can be to distinguish criticism of the position from criticism of themselves.

Institutions can encourage the better form of commitment. Researchers can preregister studies and invite replication; advocacy groups can ask affected communities whether a policy is working. Such practices make criticism a service to the underlying goal rather than an act of disloyalty.

Commitment by itself predicts neither openness nor defensiveness. People become their own best critics when they care more about a principle or outcome than about being proved right. That is a demanding habit, not an automatic consequence of conviction.

topic: Some people believe that society should try to save every plant and animal species, despite the expense to humans in effort, time, and financial well-being. Others believe that society need not make extraordinary efforts, especially at a great cost in money and jobs, to save endangered species.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss which view more closely aligns with your own position and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should address both of the views presented.
essay:
I favor serious efforts to protect endangered species, but I align more closely with the view that society need not make every extraordinary effort regardless of human cost. The first view rightly recognizes that extinction is irreversible; the second rightly asks who must pay and whether an intervention can work.

When a species declines because a factory pollutes its habitat, requiring the factory to reduce the discharge and restore the area is reasonable even if the work is costly. The species may support a wider ecosystem, and the polluter has a responsibility to repair harm. Conservation can also protect water, soil, and other resources on which people rely.

But consider a proposal to close the only employer in a poor region immediately, while evidence suggests that the species could not recover without changes across a much larger area. A symbolic closure could impose severe hardship without saving the animal. Officials should examine alternatives such as phased changes, habitat corridors, and support for workers. If the chance of success is negligible, funds may prevent more loss elsewhere.

The disagreement should not be reduced to caring about animals versus caring about people. Many communities depend on healthy ecosystems, and some conservation costs can be distributed more fairly through national funding. Conversely, a policy can be environmentally earnest while unfair to those who have few other options.

The first view supplies a strong presumption against avoidable extinction. The second reminds us that resources and human needs are real. I would require a credible conservation benefit and a fair plan for the people affected before undertaking an extraordinary intervention.

topic: Some people believe that the purpose of education is to free the mind and the spirit. Others believe that formal education tends to restrain our minds and spirits rather than set them free.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss which view more closely aligns with your own position and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should address both of the views presented.
essay:
Formal education can constrain students through rigid schedules and standardized answers, but I more closely align with the view that its purpose is to free the mind and spirit. Whether it fulfills that purpose depends on how teachers use their authority and how much room students have to question and explore.

A literature class can introduce a student to lives and ideas beyond her own experience. When she compares interpretations of a novel and supports her reading with evidence, she practices forming an independent judgment. A science course can offer similar freedom by teaching her to test a claim rather than accept a confident speaker's word. Knowledge expands the choices a person can imagine.

The opposing view describes real failures. A school that rewards only memorized answers may teach students to avoid original questions. Strict tracking can tell children early that certain subjects are not for them. Under those conditions, formal education can narrow ambition and suppress curiosity. The criticism is especially persuasive when institutions confuse obedience with learning.

Yet abandoning formal education would not automatically create freedom. Without access to books, expert guidance, and disciplined practice, many students would be limited to what their immediate surroundings provide. A well-run school offers structure as a foundation for inquiry, not a cage. It can teach necessary skills while inviting students to challenge explanations.

I therefore judge education by the independence it helps students build. Rules and curricula can be useful, but their success lies in producing people able to think, create, and revise their beliefs beyond the classroom.

topic: Some people believe it is often necessary, even desirable, for political leaders to withhold information from the public. Others believe that the public has a right to be fully informed.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss which view more closely aligns with your own position and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should address both of the views presented.
essay:
The public has a strong claim to information about decisions made in its name. I align more closely with the view that people should be fully informed, though limited secrecy can be justified when disclosure would create a specific, serious harm.

Suppose a government is considering a new tax. Citizens need to know the expected costs, the evidence behind the proposal, and who will benefit. Without those details, they cannot evaluate representatives or challenge faulty assumptions. A leader who conceals poor results merely to avoid criticism abuses public trust. Transparency can also let journalists and researchers catch mistakes before they become permanent policy.

The case for temporary secrecy is different when revealing a rescue operation's exact location would put hostages at risk. Negotiators may need time to act without broadcasting their plans. A government might also protect the identity of a person who reported corruption. These exceptions should be narrow, documented, and reviewed after the danger has passed.

Supporters of broad secrecy argue that the public may misinterpret preliminary information. That risk is real, but the remedy is explanation rather than routine withholding. Officials can distinguish uncertain evidence from settled findings and say what they do not yet know. Delayed disclosure should not become an indefinite shield for embarrassment.

The two views identify competing duties: protecting people from immediate harm and enabling them to govern themselves. The latter should be the normal rule. Secrecy is defensible only when leaders can explain a concrete reason, limit its duration, and remain accountable for what they hid.

topic: Claim: Universities should require every student to take a variety of courses outside the student's major field of study. Reason: Acquiring knowledge of various academic disciplines is the best way to become truly educated.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim and the reason on which that claim is based.
essay:
I agree that universities should require some study outside a major, but I do not accept the reason's claim that exposure to many disciplines is the single best way to become truly educated. Breadth matters when students learn to connect ideas, not when they merely collect unrelated credits.

An engineering student who studies ethics may consider how a design affects people who cannot afford it. A historian who learns statistics can judge whether a striking numerical claim reflects a genuine trend. Such courses can expose blind spots within a major and help graduates communicate across fields. That supports a modest breadth requirement.

Yet a student can sample six disciplines superficially and leave without the ability to reason carefully in any of them. Sustained work in one subject teaches how to evaluate evidence, revise a claim, and persist through difficulty. Practical experience and conversations outside class also contribute to education. The reason exaggerates breadth by treating it as sufficient.

A rigid requirement can impose extra cost on students with limited time or money. Universities should offer choices, ensure the courses are taught seriously, and keep enough space for depth. Some interdisciplinary courses might serve both goals better than a checklist of introductory surveys.

The claim is sound in a qualified form because students may not seek unfamiliar perspectives on their own. The reason is partly persuasive because breadth expands intellectual tools, but genuine education requires depth, integration, and the capacity to keep learning.

topic: Young people should be encouraged to pursue long-term, realistic goals rather than seek immediate fame and recognition.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the statement and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the statement might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
essay:
Long-term, realistic goals usually offer young people a better foundation than the pursuit of immediate fame. I agree with the recommendation, while recognizing that ambition and public recognition can sometimes support valuable work.

A teenager who wants to become a musician may be tempted to measure progress only by online views. A practical plan would include regular practice, feedback, performances, and enough education to adapt if early auditions fail. These steps are less exciting than a viral clip, but they develop abilities the student can control. Recognition may follow; it cannot substitute for the craft.

Long-term goals need not mean choosing the safest familiar occupation. A young researcher may set a demanding goal of developing affordable medical technology. It is realistic if she understands the training, time, and uncertainty involved and adjusts the plan as she learns. Young people should be encouraged to attempt difficult work, not taught to avoid all risk.

There are circumstances in which immediate visibility can be useful. An activist may use a popular post to draw attention to an urgent problem, and an artist may find an audience online. The concern is treating popularity as proof of achievement or making it the only objective. Attention is unstable and often shaped by forces outside the creator's control.

Mentors should help young people translate aspiration into milestones and reflect on setbacks. Such guidance respects ambition more than promises of instant success. Fame may be a byproduct, but an enduring goal gives effort direction when the audience moves on.

topic: Governments should not fund any scientific research whose consequences are unclear.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss your views on the policy and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider the possible consequences of implementing the policy and explain how these consequences shape your position.
essay:
If a government funded only scientific research with predictable consequences, it would abandon much of the basic inquiry from which later advances grow. I disagree with the recommendation that it should refuse all funding when outcomes are unclear. Uncertainty is often a reason to investigate, although foreseeable hazards still require safeguards.

Early work on the properties of materials may have no immediate product attached. A scientist studying how a substance conducts electricity could eventually contribute to a medical device or a more efficient power system. Neither application need be obvious at the time of the grant. Private investors often prefer projects with quicker returns, so public funding can be especially valuable for questions whose benefits are uncertain or distant.

Unclear benefits should not be confused with uncontrolled risks. If a proposed experiment might release a dangerous pathogen, the government can require independent safety review, secure facilities, and a credible containment plan. It might decline funding if these conditions cannot be met. That decision rests on a serious potential harm, rather than merely on an inability to predict the discovery. Research with human participants likewise requires consent and monitoring even when its scientific value is promising.

Public budgets are finite, and agencies must compare proposals. They can evaluate the importance of the question, the strength of the methods, and the investigators' ability to learn from unexpected results. They should not demand a guarantee that no honest researcher could provide. A portfolio can include applied projects with near-term goals and exploratory projects that may fail or open new directions.

The proposal mistakes uncertainty for futility. Government should be prudent about safety and spending, but it should finance well-designed research precisely because learning what is not yet known is a public good.

topic: Knowing about the past cannot help people to make important decisions today.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the statement and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the statement might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
essay:
The past cannot provide a ready-made answer to every modern problem, but it can help people make important decisions. I disagree with the categorical claim because historical cases reveal consequences, institutions, and recurring patterns of human behavior.

A city deciding how to respond to a flood can examine previous disasters to learn which evacuation messages reached residents and which neighborhoods lacked transport. Today's climate and infrastructure may differ, so the old plan should not simply be copied. Still, ignoring those records would waste hard-won knowledge. They help officials ask better questions about present vulnerabilities.

History can also caution against policies that sound attractive in the abstract. A government considering a new public-health measure can study how earlier campaigns gained trust or provoked resistance. The point is not that citizens today will behave exactly like their predecessors; it is that institutions can learn why a policy failed under particular conditions.

The strongest objection is that modern technology and global connections create unprecedented situations. A past case may be a poor analogy if its relevant causes differ. Decision makers must test the comparison rather than cite a historical slogan. This limitation makes careful history more valuable, not useless: it teaches people to identify what changed and what persisted.

Good decisions combine evidence from the present with knowledge of how similar choices unfolded before. The past is neither an instruction manual nor a burden to discard. It is a source of questions and warnings that can improve judgment when used with attention to context.

topic: In this age of intensive media coverage, it is no longer possible for a society to regard any living man or woman as a hero.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the statement and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the statement might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
essay:
Intensive media scrutiny makes it harder to sustain a flawless public image, but a flawless image is not required for heroism. I disagree that society can no longer regard a living person as a hero. It can recognize exceptional service while remaining willing to revise its judgment.

A firefighter who repeatedly risks her life to rescue others may be celebrated by the people she has helped. Her actions are visible now; waiting for a future historian to confirm them would be unnecessary. If reporting later reveals misconduct in another part of her life, that information should be investigated. Admiration for a courageous act need not turn into permission to ignore wrongdoing.

Media coverage serves an important purpose when it uncovers false reputations. A political leader may be praised for generosity while secretly diverting public funds. Investigative journalism can prevent misplaced trust. Yet constant coverage also rewards sensational stories and may amplify a minor mistake beyond its importance. Readers should judge evidence and proportion rather than assume every headline is a final verdict.

The claim becomes plausible only if “hero” means a person beyond moral criticism. That standard would eliminate most historical heroes too, once their lives are examined carefully. A better standard praises specific commitments or actions and acknowledges limitations.

Contemporary societies should resist uncritical hero worship, especially around powerful people. But scrutiny can make admiration more honest. Living heroes are possible when the praise is precise, provisional, and compatible with accountability.

topic: We can usually learn much more from people whose views we share than from people whose views contradict our own.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the statement and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the statement might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
essay:
People who share our views can help us develop an idea, but those who challenge us often reveal its weaknesses. I disagree that we usually learn much more from agreement than from disagreement.

A student proposing a ban on cars in a town center may learn useful arguments from classmates who already support the plan. A delivery driver who asks how supplies will reach shops, however, introduces a problem the group overlooked. The student can adjust the policy to include loading hours or reconsider its scope. That challenge makes the proposal more informed.

Disagreement is not automatically educational. If participants mock one another or refuse evidence, a conversation can become defensive and unproductive. A teacher or moderator can ask each person to restate the other's concern accurately before responding. That practice turns an opposing view into a question to investigate rather than a personal attack.

Agreement has a role in building trust and combining knowledge. A team working toward a shared goal can make progress rapidly when members understand one another's assumptions. Yet shared assumptions can also allow errors to pass untested.

The amount we learn depends less on whether a person's conclusion matches ours than on the quality of the reasons they provide and our willingness to consider them. We need both collaborators who develop an idea and critics who test whether it survives contact with other experiences.

topic: The most effective way to understand contemporary culture is to analyze the trends of its youth.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the statement and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the statement might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
essay:
Young people's choices can reveal emerging habits, but analyzing youth alone is not the most effective way to understand a whole culture. I partly disagree with the claim because culture is produced across generations and institutions.

The music, language, and online communities popular with young people can show how new tools are being used and which social questions attract attention. A researcher observing students' use of short videos may learn how information and humor travel. These trends can signal changes that later spread to older groups.

Yet a focus on youth may miss the forces shaping those trends. Employers determine work schedules; governments regulate schools and media; older family members transmit languages and customs. The same young person may use new slang with friends and follow longstanding rituals at home. To understand the culture, a researcher must examine both experiences and the relationships between them.

Youth trends can also be fleeting. A widely shared fashion may disappear within months, while less visible practices such as caregiving or neighborhood cooperation endure. Counting posts would not tell us which matters most to people's lives.

Studying young people is valuable, especially for seeing cultural change early. It becomes misleading when their most visible tastes are treated as a portrait of everyone. A fuller understanding compares generations, material conditions, and institutions as well as the trends that attract attention.

topic: People's attitudes are determined more by their immediate situation or surroundings than by society as a whole.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the statement and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the statement might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
essay:
Immediate surroundings strongly influence how people think and act, but attitudes are also shaped by the larger society in which those surroundings exist. I disagree that the local situation generally matters more; its influence is often a channel for broader norms.

A new employee may become more willing to speak up in a workplace where colleagues invite questions. In another office, the same person might remain silent after seeing criticism punished. The immediate environment changes what feels safe and acceptable. This can explain differences between people who share a national culture.

Yet the workplaces themselves are shaped by social rules about hierarchy, gender, and labor. An employee's attitudes toward authority may come from family, school, and public debate long before the first day on the job. A local office can reinforce or challenge those influences, but it does not exist outside them.

Attitudes also vary by issue. Someone might change a view about recycling after living near polluted water, while a deeply held religious belief remains stable across several moves. A single causal ranking cannot account for both cases. Long-term experience and immediate events interact.

The claim rightly warns against assuming that a broad label such as nationality explains every person's beliefs. To understand an attitude, however, we should ask how the local setting was formed and what wider values the individual brought into it. Surroundings and society work together rather than compete as independent causes.

topic: Nations should suspend government funding for the arts when significant numbers of their citizens are hungry or unemployed.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the recommendation and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, describe specific circumstances in which adopting the recommendation would or would not be advantageous and explain how these examples shape your position.
essay:
A government facing hunger or unemployment should give urgent needs high priority. I nevertheless disagree that it must suspend all arts funding whenever significant numbers of people struggle. The sensible question is what each expenditure accomplishes and what would actually be gained by cutting it.

If a city plans an expensive commemorative sculpture while food programs face an immediate shortfall, postponing the sculpture may be justified. People cannot be asked to accept preventable hunger for a prestige project. Budget choices should be open to scrutiny, and the burden of defending discretionary spending rises in a crisis.

But an arts program can provide jobs for performers, builders, teachers, and venue staff. A free library performance or community workshop may also be accessible to families who cannot pay for private entertainment. Eliminating a modest program may save little while reducing work and public life. The mere coexistence of hardship and arts funding does not prove that one caused the other.

A government should compare costs, urgency, and impact. It might defer lavish projects while preserving low-cost arts education and employment programs. It should also examine larger parts of the budget instead of treating culture as the only flexible item.

The recommendation is strongest when a specific arts expense clearly displaces essential aid. As an automatic national rule, it ignores the ways cultural funding can serve people, including those who are hungry or unemployed. Basic needs come first, but priorities require evidence rather than a blanket suspension.

topic: All parents should be required to volunteer time to their children's schools.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the recommendation and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, describe specific circumstances in which adopting the recommendation would or would not be advantageous and explain how these examples shape your position.
essay:
Parents' participation can strengthen schools, but requiring every parent to volunteer time would unfairly penalize families whose schedules or circumstances make it difficult. I disagree with a universal mandate, while supporting more accessible ways for parents to contribute.

A parent who can help organize a reading event may build relationships with teachers and other families. Schools benefit when adults share skills, listen to concerns, and understand what students need. Such involvement can make the school a stronger community.

Yet a single parent working irregular shifts may be unable to attend a daytime event without losing wages. A caregiver responsible for a sick relative may face a similar barrier. If volunteering is compulsory, the policy could label precisely those families as less committed, even when they support their children every evening. It might also create administrative work for schools to monitor hours rather than help students.

Schools can offer flexible options, including remote tasks, evening meetings, or short contributions when parents are able. More importantly, they should welcome communication without measuring care by unpaid labor. Some families may need translation or transport before participation is possible.

The recommendation is advantageous where it encourages partnership, but its compulsory form ignores unequal capacity. Schools should invite, support, and value parental involvement without making time away from paid work a condition of being considered a responsible parent.

topic: Colleges and universities should require their students to spend at least one semester studying in a foreign country.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the recommendation and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, describe specific circumstances in which adopting the recommendation would or would not be advantageous and explain how these examples shape your position.
essay:
A semester abroad can broaden a student's perspective, but requiring it of every university student would impose unequal costs and may not serve every course of study. I disagree with the universal requirement while supporting well-funded opportunities to study overseas.

Living in another country can challenge assumptions that a tourist visit leaves untouched. A student may learn a language through daily use and discover different approaches to public transport, education, or family life. A semester offers time to form relationships rather than collect impressions. Those are strong reasons for universities to make exchanges accessible.

The requirement becomes harder to defend for a student who supports family members, has a disability that requires particular services, or cannot afford travel and housing. Scholarships can solve some problems but not every responsibility. A nursing student may also need a placement whose accreditation and clinical hours cannot easily be transferred. Delaying graduation for an exchange could do more harm than good.

Universities can encourage international learning through partnerships, remote collaboration, visiting scholars, or study of other cultures at home. These experiences are not identical to residence abroad, but they can meet some of the same educational aims. A voluntary semester with financial and academic support gives students the chance to choose the deeper immersion when it fits.

The recommendation is valuable as an aspiration for broad access, not as an inflexible graduation condition. An opportunity is most educational when students can take it without unreasonable sacrifice and connect it to their goals.

topic: Teachers' salaries should be based on the academic performance of their students.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the recommendation and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, describe specific circumstances in which adopting the recommendation would or would not be advantageous and explain how these examples shape your position.
essay:
Student achievement matters, but tying teachers' salaries directly to their students' test performance would reward and penalize factors outside a teacher's control. I disagree with the proposal as a principal pay rule. Schools should evaluate teachers' work, but an examination score is too narrow a measure of it.

Imagine two teachers who prepare equally thoughtful lessons. One teaches a small class with reliable internet and substantial support at home; the other works with students who have missed school because of illness or unstable housing. Their final scores may differ even if the second teacher helped students make greater progress. Paying the first more on raw outcomes would mistake unequal starting conditions for unequal effort or skill.

A strict score-based system can also distort instruction. If a teacher's income depends on one test, it becomes rational to spend extra time on the questions most likely to appear and less on discussion, writing, or students whose scores are unlikely to cross a threshold. A science class might memorize definitions rather than learn to design an experiment. The apparent improvement in measured performance could conceal a decline in education.

Supporters of performance pay rightly want accountability. Schools should not assume that every teacher is effective merely because they have taught for many years. Classroom observations, feedback from students, evidence of growth over time, and review of lesson plans can reveal strengths and weaknesses. Each measure has limitations, so several should be considered together and used to provide support as well as make pay decisions.

Teachers influence learning deeply, and their work deserves serious evaluation. Yet salary rules should avoid punishing those who take difficult assignments or rewarding a narrow form of test preparation. A fair system would value teaching quality and student progress in context rather than reduce both to a single score.

topic: It is no longer possible for a society to regard any living man or woman as a hero.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim. In developing and supporting your position, be sure to address the most compelling reasons and/or examples that could be used to challenge your position.
essay:
A living person can still be a hero even when public scrutiny reveals imperfections. I disagree with the assertion because heroism need not mean a life beyond criticism.

A community may honor a volunteer who repeatedly delivers supplies after a disaster. Residents know the benefit now and can appreciate the courage or persistence involved. If new evidence shows that the volunteer also treated colleagues unfairly, they should address that harm. It does not require pretending that the relief work never happened.

The claim reflects a reasonable fear of idealization. Public figures can cultivate images that hide wrongdoing, and modern reporting can expose contradictions. But the same scrutiny can help communities praise more accurately: a leader's self-promotion may fade while the quiet work of local organizers becomes visible. Investigation changes judgments; it does not make all admiration impossible.

A useful concept of a hero concerns exceptional actions or sustained service under difficulty, not moral perfection. People can recognize those qualities while withholding unconditional trust and holding a person accountable in other roles. Later generations may change the assessment, just as they revise views of historical figures.

Society should be cautious about placing anyone above examination. It need not wait until death to acknowledge sacrifice and service. The possibility of correction is a reason for modest, evidence-based praise, not a reason to abandon the word “hero.”

topic: Some people believe that in order to thrive, a society must put its own overall success before the well-being of its individual citizens. Others believe that the well- being of a society can only be measured by the general welfare of all its people.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss which view more closely aligns with your own position and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should address both of the views presented.
essay:
I align more closely with the view that a society's success should be measured by the welfare of its people. The competing view rightly recognizes that societies need productive institutions, but “overall success” is empty if it requires sacrificing the citizens it is supposed to serve.

A government might boast of economic growth while many families cannot obtain safe housing or basic healthcare. The total figure says little about who benefits. A more convincing account would examine whether people can live securely, learn, and take part in public life. An economy is a means to those ends, not an achievement that excuses their absence.

The first view has a serious point when it asks individuals to contribute to shared projects. Taxes can support public infrastructure, and temporary inconvenience may be justified during an emergency. A community could not function if every person demanded an immediate private benefit from every decision. Yet these sacrifices need fair distribution and a credible connection to people's long-term welfare.

The second view should not be reduced to a single average. A high mean income could hide severe deprivation among a minority. Welfare includes opportunity, rights, and protection for vulnerable people as well as material prosperity.

The views are therefore related but not equally persuasive as standards of judgment. Collective projects are worthwhile when they enable citizens to flourish across time. A society that records impressive aggregate achievements while neglecting the people who made them possible has confused its instruments with its purpose.

topic: Claim: Any piece of information referred to as a fact should be mistrusted, since it may well be proven false in the future. Reason: Much of the information that people assume is factual actually turns out to be inaccurate.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim and the reason on which that claim is based.
essay:
I disagree that every statement called a fact should be mistrusted. The reason is partly true: beliefs once treated as certain have sometimes been corrected. But a history of error calls for evidence and appropriate confidence, not indiscriminate suspicion.

A physician might once have attributed an illness to a single cause, then change that explanation when better tests become available. Scientific correction is a strength of inquiry. It should encourage patients to ask how a claim was tested and whether experts agree. It should not lead them to treat an established finding about sanitation as no more reliable than an unsupported rumor.

Facts also differ in kind. The date of a recorded election can be checked against multiple documents. A claim that one policy caused a rise in employment depends on models and competing explanations. Both can be investigated, but they deserve different degrees of confidence and different language. Calling them all untrustworthy ignores these distinctions.

The reason does not prove the claim. Even if many assumptions prove false, others survive repeated attempts at correction. We rely on such knowledge to build bridges, administer medicine, and make everyday decisions. Complete mistrust would make learning from evidence impossible.

A more useful habit is calibrated trust: seek sources, understand uncertainty, and revise beliefs when stronger evidence appears. The possibility of future correction should make people intellectually humble, not unable to recognize a well-supported fact.

topic: Claim: Nations should suspend government funding for the arts when significant numbers of their citizens are hungry or unemployed. Reason: It is inappropriate — and, perhaps, even cruel — to use public resources to fund the arts when people's basic needs are not being met.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim and the reason on which that claim is based.
essay:
I agree that a government should prioritize urgent needs when citizens are hungry or unemployed, and the reason rightly emphasizes the cruelty of neglecting those needs. I disagree, however, that this requires suspending all public arts funding. A budget must be judged by the effects of particular choices.

If officials fund a lavish festival while emergency food services are being cut for lack of money, redirecting that expense is justified. The reason applies directly: a discretionary celebration cannot be defended at the expense of preventable hunger. Public resources must respond to immediate suffering.

But a small arts grant may pay local teachers and technicians, offer free classes, and support work in a struggling neighborhood. Canceling it could increase unemployment while saving too little to address food insecurity. Arts funding is not necessarily a transfer from the poor to an elite; its benefits and recipients vary. Governments should compare programs and seek fair ways to protect both livelihoods and access to culture.

The reason also depends on a false choice if other spending is available. Officials should examine procurement, subsidies, and large capital projects before asserting that every gallery or community theater must close. This does not give the arts automatic protection; it requires an honest accounting of costs and alternatives.

The claim captures a moral priority but turns it into a rigid rule. Governments should meet basic needs first and defer projects that genuinely compete with those needs. They need not eliminate useful cultural programs merely because hardship exists somewhere in the country.

topic: Claim: Many problems of modern society cannot be solved by laws and the legal system. Reason: Laws cannot change what is in people's hearts or minds.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim and the reason on which that claim is based.
essay:
I agree that many social problems cannot be solved by law alone, but I disagree with the reason if it implies that laws cannot influence attitudes. Rules cannot instantly change a person's beliefs; they can still change conduct, incentives, and the experiences through which beliefs develop.

Consider discrimination in hiring. A legal prohibition cannot make every employer fair-minded. It can provide a remedy for rejected applicants, require transparent procedures, and make discriminatory decisions costly. Over time, a workplace in which people collaborate across backgrounds may challenge assumptions some employees initially held. The law works partly through conduct before it works through conviction.

At the same time, enforcement has limits. A community plagued by distrust will not become cooperative merely because a statute demands respect. Schools, families, civic groups, and economic opportunities also matter. A rule that is poorly enforced or widely misunderstood may even invite evasion. Reformers should pair legal protection with education and institutional change.

The claim is strongest when it rejects the idea that passing a bill completes a reform. The reason is too absolute: laws may not reach directly into minds, but they alter the conditions in which people form habits and judgments. Civil rights protections, for example, matter both because they constrain harmful behavior and because they make participation possible for those previously excluded.

Social change usually needs more than one instrument. Law can set boundaries and provide recourse, while public discussion and daily experience help transform beliefs. Its inability to do everything is not evidence that it can do nothing.

topic: Educators should take students' interests into account when planning the content of the courses they teach.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the recommendation and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, describe specific circumstances in which adopting the recommendation would or would not be advantageous and explain how these examples shape your position.
essay:
Educators should consider students' interests when planning a course, because relevant questions can motivate sustained work. I agree with the recommendation, provided that interest informs how essential material is taught rather than deciding whether it is taught at all.

A geography teacher whose students ask about flooding in their town can use local maps to introduce watersheds, land use, and data interpretation. Learners have a reason to compare evidence because the issue affects streets they know. The teacher still chooses methods and concepts that make the inquiry rigorous.

The danger is assuming that students already know every topic worth studying. A class may express little interest in probability because it has not seen how probability clarifies medical risks or weather forecasts. The teacher can make the subject accessible and show its relevance instead of dropping it. Education should develop interests as well as respond to them.

Student feedback can reveal when an example is confusing or when a project invites genuine effort. But a curriculum also has public purposes: preparing students to reason, communicate, and understand unfamiliar ideas. Those purposes require professional judgment and some shared standards.

The recommendation works best as a partnership. Students contribute questions and report what helps them engage; educators connect those questions to important knowledge and challenge students to move beyond what already feels comfortable.

topic: The primary goal of technological advancement should be to increase people's efficiency so that they have more leisure time.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the statement and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the statement might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
essay:
Technological advancement can free time, but maximizing efficiency should not be its primary goal in every case. I disagree with the proposed single purpose because some technologies are valuable chiefly for safety, access, or understanding, even if they do not increase leisure.

An automated scheduling system might reduce repetitive office work and allow employees to leave on time. That is a genuine gain if the saved hours belong to workers. If managers instead increase targets until everyone is just as busy, efficiency has risen without delivering the promised leisure. Institutions decide how technological gains are shared.

Other innovations serve a different aim. A wheelchair with improved controls may help its user travel independently, even if a trip takes just as long. A scientific instrument may make a rare disease easier to diagnose while requiring more careful work from clinicians. Judging either solely by hours saved would miss the benefit.

The goal of leisure is also more complicated than an empty calendar. People may value meaningful work and use technology to improve its quality rather than eliminate it. The relevant question is whether a tool expands human choice and well-being, including the ability to rest.

Efficiency is an important design criterion when wasteful tasks consume people's days. It should be evaluated alongside safety, fairness, access, and the purposes of the activity. More leisure is a possible reward of progress, not a universal definition of it.

topic: Educators should base their assessment of students' learning not on students' grasp of facts but on the ability to explain the ideas, trends, and concepts that those facts illustrate.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the recommendation and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, describe specific circumstances in which adopting the recommendation would or would not be advantageous and explain how these examples shape your position.
essay:
Students should be able to explain the ideas that facts illustrate, but an assessment that disregards factual grasp would be incomplete. I partly agree with the recommendation because understanding requires both evidence and the ability to interpret it.

In a history exam, recalling a date alone tells a teacher little about whether a student understands a political change. Asking students to compare two documents and explain what they show about the change reveals more. Yet an answer that places the documents in the wrong century can also be misleading. The relevant facts anchor the interpretation.

Science offers the same lesson. A student who can define photosynthesis but cannot explain how light and carbon dioxide affect a plant has memorized without understanding. Another who offers an elegant explanation while misreporting the experiment's results has failed to use evidence accurately. A strong assessment asks for both a correct observation and a reasoned account of it.

There are practical constraints. Short tests can check foundational knowledge efficiently, while projects or written explanations show how students apply it. Teachers should combine formats rather than declare facts irrelevant. Feedback can identify whether a mistake arises from missing knowledge or a flawed concept.

The recommendation usefully resists rote memorization as the sole measure of learning. Its absolute contrast is false, however. Ideas, trends, and concepts become convincing when students can connect them to accurate facts and explain why those facts matter.

topic: Unfortunately, in contemporary society, creating an appealing image has become more important than the reality or truth behind that image.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the statement and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the statement might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
essay:
In many settings an appealing image receives more immediate attention than the truth behind it. I partly agree with the statement, but “more important” describes an incentive created by particular media and institutions rather than a complete account of contemporary society.

An applicant might present a polished online profile that suggests expertise without showing completed work. A company can advertise a green product while concealing the pollution involved in producing it. When viewers see only a brief post or advertisement, appearance may win the first judgment. The pressure to seem successful can encourage people to manage impressions rather than improve what they offer.

The reality eventually matters. An employer who checks references and asks for a work sample can discover whether the applicant has the claimed skills. Customers who compare independent evidence can test a company's environmental promise. Journalism, audits, and long-term relationships create incentives for honesty, although they require time and access to information.

Images are not inherently deceptive. A clear presentation can help a useful idea reach people who would otherwise overlook it. The problem arises when institutions reward attention alone and neglect verification. A scientist explaining a result vividly can be both accurate and engaging.

The claim captures a genuine distortion in a crowded information environment. It is too broad if it suggests that reality has lost its power. The remedy is not to reject communication, but to make it easier and more worthwhile to test the claims beneath the attractive surface.

topic: The effectiveness of a country's leaders is best measured by examining the well- being of that country's citizens.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim. In developing and supporting your position, be sure to address the most compelling reasons and/or examples that could be used to challenge your position.
essay:
A leader's effectiveness should be judged substantially by how citizens fare. I agree with the statement, provided that well-being is measured over time and that leaders are held responsible only for effects they could reasonably influence.

A mayor who improves access to clean water and reliable clinics has produced results that matter more than a polished speech or a high approval rating. Looking at infant health, service availability, and whether poorer districts benefit can reveal whether policy reached people. Such outcomes are a useful check on a leader's promises.

Yet a sudden drought or global recession may harm citizens despite competent action. Conversely, a leader can inherit favorable conditions and claim credit for prosperity already underway. Evaluation should compare choices with realistic alternatives and consider the resources and constraints the leader faced. It should also watch for policies that improve a short-term statistic while creating future debt or environmental damage.

Well-being includes more than income. Safety, rights, education, and the ability to participate in public life all matter. A government that raises average output while silencing criticism cannot claim unqualified success from the economic figure alone.

Citizen welfare is the best starting point because leadership is a public responsibility, not a personal performance. A careful judgment links outcomes to decisions, considers distribution and duration, and asks whether citizens are better able to lead secure and meaningful lives.

topic: All parents should be required to volunteer time to their children's schools.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim. In developing and supporting your position, be sure to address the most compelling reasons and/or examples that could be used to challenge your position.
essay:
Parents' participation can strengthen schools, but requiring every parent to volunteer time would unfairly penalize families whose schedules or circumstances make it difficult. I disagree with a universal mandate, while supporting more accessible ways for parents to contribute.

A parent who can help organize a reading event may build relationships with teachers and other families. Schools benefit when adults share skills, listen to concerns, and understand what students need. Such involvement can make the school a stronger community.

Yet a single parent working irregular shifts may be unable to attend a daytime event without losing wages. A caregiver responsible for a sick relative may face a similar barrier. If volunteering is compulsory, the policy could label precisely those families as less committed, even when they support their children every evening. It might also create administrative work for schools to monitor hours rather than help students.

Schools can offer flexible options, including remote tasks, evening meetings, or short contributions when parents are able. More importantly, they should welcome communication without measuring care by unpaid labor. Some families may need translation or transport before participation is possible.

The recommendation is advantageous where it encourages partnership, but its compulsory form ignores unequal capacity. Schools should invite, support, and value parental involvement without making time away from paid work a condition of being considered a responsible parent.

topic: A nation should require all of its students to study the same national curriculum until they enter college.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim. In developing and supporting your position, be sure to address the most compelling reasons and/or examples that could be used to challenge your position.
essay:
A common national curriculum can guarantee access to important knowledge, but requiring every student to study exactly the same material until college would ignore local needs and individual development. I partly disagree with the statement.

Shared instruction in literacy, mathematics, science, and civic history can protect students whose schools might otherwise offer a thin education. A family moving between regions should not find that a child has missed an essential prerequisite. Common standards also give the public a basis for asking whether schools serve students fairly.

Uniformity becomes harmful when it prescribes every text, project, and pace. A coastal community may use local ecology to teach scientific methods; another may study water scarcity. Both can meet the same underlying standard. Students who need additional language support or advanced work may require different routes to mastery. A rigid curriculum could force teachers to move on before one group understands or leave another unchallenged.

National content can also become a political instrument if one authority decides that only a single interpretation of history may be taught. Opportunities to compare sources and question claims are part of a sound civic education.

A better policy establishes a core of knowledge and skills, then gives schools room to adapt examples, offer electives, and support different learners. Equal educational opportunity requires shared expectations, but it does not require identical lessons for every child.

topic: Colleges and universities should require their students to spend at least one semester studying in a foreign country.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim. In developing and supporting your position, be sure to address the most compelling reasons and/or examples that could be used to challenge your position.
essay:
A semester abroad can broaden a student's perspective, but requiring it of every university student would impose unequal costs and may not serve every course of study. I disagree with the universal requirement while supporting well-funded opportunities to study overseas.

Living in another country can challenge assumptions that a tourist visit leaves untouched. A student may learn a language through daily use and discover different approaches to public transport, education, or family life. A semester offers time to form relationships rather than collect impressions. Those are strong reasons for universities to make exchanges accessible.

The requirement becomes harder to defend for a student who supports family members, has a disability that requires particular services, or cannot afford travel and housing. Scholarships can solve some problems but not every responsibility. A nursing student may also need a placement whose accreditation and clinical hours cannot easily be transferred. Delaying graduation for an exchange could do more harm than good.

Universities can encourage international learning through partnerships, remote collaboration, visiting scholars, or study of other cultures at home. These experiences are not identical to residence abroad, but they can meet some of the same educational aims. A voluntary semester with financial and academic support gives students the chance to choose the deeper immersion when it fits.

The recommendation is valuable as an aspiration for broad access, not as an inflexible graduation condition. An opportunity is most educational when students can take it without unreasonable sacrifice and connect it to their goals.

topic: Educational institutions should actively encourage their students to choose fields of study in which jobs are plentiful.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss your views on the policy and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider the possible consequences of implementing the policy and explain how these consequences shape your position.
essay:
Institutions should tell students where jobs are plentiful, but they should not actively steer everyone toward those fields. I partly disagree with the statement because the number of current openings is only one part of a durable career choice.

A college may see high demand for nurses and offer accurate information about training and employment. A student who enjoys patient care might then pursue nursing with a clear sense of the work. But encouraging a student who finds clinical duties distressing simply because jobs are available would serve neither the student nor patients. Aptitude and commitment matter.

Markets also change. A program that expands rapidly to match today's vacancies may graduate a large cohort after demand has shifted. Students need adaptable skills and a realistic view of costs, not a promise that one sector will always be safe. Institutions can support internships and career exploration across fields rather than treating a job count as a command.

The opposing concern is legitimate: a college that ignores outcomes while charging high tuition can leave graduates with debt and few options. Transparent data about earnings, placement, and alternative qualifications helps students make informed decisions.

Encouragement is most useful when it connects a student's interests and abilities with credible opportunities. Institutions should make labor-market information available and help students plan, while preserving the freedom to choose a path whose value cannot be reduced to today's vacancies.

topic: People's behavior is largely determined by forces not of their own making.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim. In developing and supporting your position, be sure to address the most compelling reasons and/or examples that could be used to challenge your position.
essay:
People's circumstances shape their behavior, but they rarely remove all agency. I partly agree that forces outside a person's control have a large influence, while rejecting the idea that conduct is simply predetermined.

A child raised in a neighborhood with few safe places to play may spend less time outdoors than one with parks nearby. A worker facing unpredictable shifts may miss appointments despite caring about health. These examples show why judging outcomes without considering environment is unfair. Social policy can change behavior by changing available choices.

Yet people facing similar constraints sometimes act differently. One worker may organize colleagues to request more stable hours; another may seek a different job if one is available. Such choices do not prove that the constraints were imaginary. They show that individuals interpret situations and can respond creatively, though not everyone has equal room to do so.

The claim becomes dangerous if it excuses harmful acts as inevitable or blames disadvantaged people for failing to overcome every barrier. A more accurate account assigns responsibility in proportion to genuine options and recognizes that institutions also bear responsibility for the conditions they create.

Understanding behavior requires both levels of explanation. Forces such as poverty, norms, and policy set the stage, while habits, relationships, and decisions influence what happens within it. Effective reform expands people's choices instead of pretending either that everyone is entirely free or that no one can change.

In developing and supporting your position, you should consider the possible consequences of implementing the policy and explain how these consequences shape your position.
