topic: Although innovations such as video, computers, and the Internet seem to offer schools improved methods for instructing students, these technologies all too often distract from real learning.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the statement and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the statement might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
essay:
Digital tools can distract students, but they can also make learning more active and accessible. I disagree that video, computers, and the Internet all too often undermine real learning as a general judgment. Their effect depends on the lesson and how attention is guided.

A short video of a scientific process can let students observe something a school cannot reproduce safely. A simulation can allow them to change one variable and see the result. If the teacher then asks students to explain what happened and test a prediction, the technology supports reasoning rather than replacing it.

Distraction is a genuine risk. A student who switches between a lesson, messages, and unrelated videos may retain little. A teacher who plays a long recording without discussion can turn class into passive viewing. Schools should set clear device expectations and choose tools for specific educational purposes, not merely because they are new.

Technology also matters for access. Captions can help a learner follow a lecture, and an online resource can reach a student whose school lacks specialized materials. These benefits do not require every activity to be on a screen; reading, conversation, and hands-on work remain essential.

The statement usefully warns against mistaking novelty for progress. It overgeneralizes when it treats the medium as the cause of poor learning. The test is whether students can explain, apply, and question what they encounter, with or without a device.

topic: Universities should require every student to take a variety of courses outside the student's field of study.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss your views on the policy and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider the possible consequences of implementing the policy and explain how these consequences shape your position.
essay:
Courses beyond a major can give university students tools they would not encounter in a narrow program. I support requiring some breadth, provided the requirement leaves room for depth and does not become an inflexible checklist.

An engineering student who studies public policy may recognize that a technically efficient water system can fail if residents cannot afford access. A literature student who takes statistics may better evaluate claims about reading habits or social inequality. In both cases, the second discipline changes how the student uses the first. Universities have reason to introduce connections students might not seek on their own.

Yet extra courses have costs in tuition and time. A student already balancing work with a demanding degree might be delayed by a large set of unrelated requirements. The institution should offer meaningful choices, transfer credit where appropriate, and design courses that invite serious engagement. It should not confuse collecting credits with becoming educated.

Breadth is particularly advantageous when it complements specialization and creates informed citizens. It is less advantageous when a rigid rule prevents a student from completing essential training or imposes avoidable debt. A modest, thoughtfully chosen requirement serves the recommendation better than an indiscriminate one.

topic: The best ideas arise from a passionate interest in commonplace things.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the statement and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the statement might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
essay:
A passionate interest in ordinary things can produce striking ideas because it encourages close observation. I mostly agree with the statement, though curiosity must be joined to knowledge and testing before an idea becomes valuable.

An engineer watching people struggle with a heavy door might ask why its handle gives so little leverage. The problem is commonplace, but careful attention could lead to a more accessible design. Someone who assumes ordinary objects are already perfected may never notice the difficulty. Interest turns a routine inconvenience into a question worth investigating.

A writer can similarly find a compelling story in a family's daily journey to school. Listening closely to familiar conversations may reveal conflicts about work, care, and ambition that a more sensational setting would obscure. Originality can arise from seeing what others pass over, not merely from seeking an exotic subject.

Passion alone does not guarantee a good idea. The engineer must test whether the new handle is safe and affordable; the writer must shape observations into a coherent work. Expert knowledge helps distinguish a real gap from a misunderstanding. Interest supplies persistence through that demanding process.

The word “best” is hard to prove: some important ideas arise from urgent crises or unfamiliar places. Still, the claim offers a useful lesson. People need not wait for a grand subject before thinking creatively. They can begin by paying sustained attention to the ordinary world around them.

topic: To be an effective leader, a public official must maintain the highest ethical and moral standards.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim. In developing and supporting your position, be sure to address the most compelling reasons and/or examples that could be used to challenge your position.
essay:
Public officials need high ethical standards because they wield authority over people who may have little power to refuse their decisions. I agree that integrity is essential to effective leadership, although moral character alone cannot replace competence.

A mayor who awards contracts to friends may still deliver a visible project, but favoritism wastes public money and undermines trust. Residents may reasonably doubt later decisions even when those decisions are sound. Honest procedures, disclosure of conflicts, and willingness to correct mistakes help make cooperation possible.

An official can also be personally sincere and still govern badly. A health leader who ignores scientific evidence because of a deeply held belief may put citizens at risk. Effective leadership requires learning from experts, listening to affected communities, and managing institutions. The standard should include the ethics of how a decision is made and the skill to carry it out.

The phrase “highest ethical standards” should not demand perfection in every private choice. It should mean that officials do not abuse power, conceal important conflicts, or treat citizens as means to personal gain. Clear accountability is more useful than an image of moral purity.

When trust is damaged, even a beneficial policy becomes harder to implement. Ethical conduct is therefore practical as well as admirable. A public official needs both principled judgment and the ability to deliver results; neither can reliably substitute for the other.

topic: Claim: Imagination is a more valuable asset than experience. Reason: People who lack experience are free to imagine what is possible without the constraints of established habits and attitudes.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim and the reason on which that claim is based.
essay:
I partly disagree with the claim that imagination is more valuable than experience, and I find the reason incomplete. Inexperience can free someone from habitual assumptions, but it can also conceal obstacles that experience makes visible.

A newcomer to urban planning might imagine converting an unused road into a public garden. Veteran planners may have dismissed the idea because they are accustomed to car traffic. The proposal deserves consideration. Yet an experienced engineer can identify drainage, emergency access, and maintenance needs that the newcomer did not see. Their knowledge need not end the project; it can make the imagined garden feasible.

The reason assumes experience only constrains. It can instead supply material for creativity. A nurse who has cared for many patients may invent a simpler handoff process precisely because she has observed repeated communication failures. Without those encounters, a proposed solution might solve a problem that does not exist.

There are settings where fresh eyes are especially valuable, such as a field whose established approach repeatedly fails. People lacking experience may ask questions insiders have stopped asking. Their advantage is strongest when an institution invites those questions and then tests the resulting ideas with informed scrutiny.

Imagination generates possibilities; experience helps select, refine, and execute them. Neither quality has a fixed greater value independent of the task. The most productive teams make room for newcomers to challenge conventions and for practiced colleagues to reveal constraints and opportunities.

topic: In most professions and academic fields, imagination is more important than knowledge.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the statement and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the statement might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
essay:
Imagination allows professionals to propose alternatives, while knowledge lets them judge whether those alternatives can work. I disagree that imagination is generally more important than knowledge across most fields, although breakthroughs often require both.

A physician may imagine a new treatment after noticing that patients respond differently to an established drug. The hypothesis is valuable, but knowledge of physiology and clinical testing is necessary to distinguish a genuine effect from coincidence and to protect patients. An untested creative guess is not yet a medical advance.

In architecture, knowledge of materials and safety codes similarly constrains a design. Those constraints can stimulate rather than suppress imagination: a designer might find an elegant way to use less energy while making a building accessible. Knowing what earlier designs achieved also prevents the reinvention of failed solutions.

The claim is more persuasive when a field has become complacent. Experts can assume a problem has only one acceptable solution, and an imaginative outsider may expose that assumption. But the outsider's idea gains value when it is developed and tested against reality. Knowledge is not merely a stock of facts; it includes ways to evaluate a proposal.

No universal ranking will fit every task. Routine practice may depend more heavily on established knowledge, while a novel challenge may demand unusual imagination. Across both cases, the strongest work joins inventive possibilities with disciplined understanding.

topic: To be an effective leader, a public official must maintain the highest ethical and moral standards.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the statement and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the statement might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
essay:
Public officials need high ethical standards because they wield authority over people who may have little power to refuse their decisions. I agree that integrity is essential to effective leadership, although moral character alone cannot replace competence.

A mayor who awards contracts to friends may still deliver a visible project, but favoritism wastes public money and undermines trust. Residents may reasonably doubt later decisions even when those decisions are sound. Honest procedures, disclosure of conflicts, and willingness to correct mistakes help make cooperation possible.

An official can also be personally sincere and still govern badly. A health leader who ignores scientific evidence because of a deeply held belief may put citizens at risk. Effective leadership requires learning from experts, listening to affected communities, and managing institutions. The standard should include the ethics of how a decision is made and the skill to carry it out.

The phrase “highest ethical standards” should not demand perfection in every private choice. It should mean that officials do not abuse power, conceal important conflicts, or treat citizens as means to personal gain. Clear accountability is more useful than an image of moral purity.

When trust is damaged, even a beneficial policy becomes harder to implement. Ethical conduct is therefore practical as well as admirable. A public official needs both principled judgment and the ability to deliver results; neither can reliably substitute for the other.

topic: Critical judgment of work in any given field has little value unless it comes from someone who is an expert in that field.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the statement and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the statement might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
essay:
An expert's criticism can reveal technical flaws, but people outside a field can also make valuable judgments about its work. I disagree that criticism has little value unless it comes from an expert.

A structural engineer is well placed to evaluate whether a bridge design meets safety standards. A commuter, however, may notice that the proposed route makes the bridge difficult for pedestrians to use. The commuter cannot replace an engineering calculation, but the experience identifies a question the technical review might overlook. Both kinds of criticism matter for a public project.

Art offers a similar distinction. A film scholar may analyze editing and historical influences, while ordinary viewers can report whether a scene communicates the intended emotion or excludes an audience. Popular reaction is not an infallible measure of merit, just as specialist approval is not. The value of a judgment depends partly on what question is being asked.

Expertise is especially important where a mistake has serious consequences and the methods are hard to assess without training. Public opinion alone cannot establish whether a medicine is safe. Yet patients can still describe side effects or burdens that researchers failed to measure. Experts should test such reports rather than dismiss them because the reporters lack credentials.

A good critic offers reasons and evidence appropriate to the claim. Expertise can strengthen that contribution, but it does not grant a monopoly on observation, interpretation, or the experience of being affected by a work.

topic: Some people believe that scientific discoveries have given us a much better understanding of the world around us. Others believe that science has revealed to us that the world is infinitely more complex than we ever realized.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss which view more closely aligns with your own position and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should address both of the views presented.
essay:
Scientific discoveries have made many parts of the world more intelligible, yet each advance can reveal questions that earlier generations did not know how to ask. Of the two views, I more closely align with the claim that science has greatly improved our understanding. Discovering further complexity is evidence of that improvement, rather than proof that understanding has failed.

The history of infectious disease illustrates this progress. Before microbes were understood, a physician could observe that illness spread without reliably explaining how. Research into pathogens made it possible to identify routes of transmission, sterilize instruments, and develop targeted vaccines. Medicine still confronts complicated interactions among genes, immune systems, and environments. Those unresolved problems are real, but a patient benefits from the knowledge already gained. The ability to formulate more precise questions is itself a sign that science has moved beyond vague speculation.

Another example is weather forecasting. The atmosphere remains difficult to model because many interacting conditions affect a storm's path. Nevertheless, satellites, measurements, and mathematical models now help communities prepare for dangerous weather. A forecast is not perfect knowledge, and its uncertainty should be communicated honestly. Still, comparing a forecast with what could be known without systematic observation shows why increased awareness of complexity does not cancel practical understanding.

The second view captures an important caution. A scientific model can explain some outcomes while leaving others unresolved. In genetics, learning that DNA carries inherited information did not make it simple to predict how every trait would develop. The effects of many genes and environmental conditions can interact. This complexity should make researchers modest about claims that one discovery has explained everything. It should also motivate better experiments, rather than lead us to dismiss the explanatory power of earlier findings.

I therefore accept the second view as a description of how inquiry expands its horizon, but I find the first view more persuasive as a judgment about what science has achieved. We understand enough about microbes to prevent many infections and enough about the atmosphere to prepare for some storms, even while both fields contain open questions. Scientific progress is neither complete certainty nor an endless admission of ignorance. It is the growing ability to explain, test, predict, and act while recognizing the limits of each explanation.

topic: In any profession — business, politics, education, government — those in power should step down after five years.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim. In developing and supporting your position, be sure to address the most compelling reasons and/or examples that could be used to challenge your position.
essay:
Fixed terms can refresh an institution, but requiring every leader in business, politics, education, and government to step down after five years would ignore major differences among roles. I disagree with the universal rule.

A public official who can remain indefinitely may entrench power and discourage challengers. A term limit can protect political competition where elections or oversight are weak. Even then, a five-year threshold is arbitrary: voters may wish to retain an effective representative while removing an ineffective one earlier.

In a research institution, a director might need more than five years to build a laboratory, recruit staff, and assess a long-term project. Automatic departure could disrupt work just as it becomes productive. A struggling company, by contrast, might need a new leader after two years. Performance, succession planning, and accountability offer more relevant guides than one clock for every field.

Supporters of limits rightly fear stagnation. Institutions should develop new leaders, permit criticism, and make it possible to remove those who misuse authority. Boards, transparent evaluation, and competitive elections can help. These mechanisms should not depend solely on a fixed tenure.

The value of turnover depends on how leadership is chosen and what work remains unfinished. Some roles warrant term limits; others benefit from continuity with strong oversight. A universal five-year rule mistakes a useful safeguard for a complete theory of leadership.

topic: Requiring university students to take a variety of courses outside their major fields of study is the best way to ensure that students become truly educated.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the statement and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the statement might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
essay:
Courses outside a major can broaden a student's judgment, but they are not by themselves the best guarantee of becoming truly educated. I partly agree with the statement: universities should require some breadth while ensuring depth and the ability to connect fields.

An engineer who studies public policy may notice that a technically efficient water system could be unaffordable to the people it serves. A historian who learns statistics can evaluate numerical evidence more carefully. In both cases, an unfamiliar course changes how the student works in the major. If universities left all breadth to chance, many students would never discover those connections.

Yet a checklist of unrelated introductory courses can be completed with little understanding. Sustained study within a major teaches students to investigate a question, test evidence, and revise a conclusion. Practical work and discussion across backgrounds add further dimensions. A requirement cannot ensure education merely by increasing the number of departments on a transcript.

Time and cost also matter. A student with a demanding professional program should be able to choose courses that complement it without unnecessary delay. Universities can offer integrated projects and flexible options while holding students to serious standards.

Breadth is a valuable part of education, especially when it challenges narrow assumptions. It works best alongside disciplinary depth and active reasoning. A variety of courses is a promising method, not a sufficient test of whether a graduate is truly educated.

topic: Claim: The surest indicator of a great nation is not the achievements of its rulers, artists, or scientists. Reason: The surest indicator of a great nation is actually the welfare of all its people.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim and the reason on which that claim is based.
essay:
I agree with the claim that a nation's greatness is better indicated by the welfare of its people than by the achievements of famous individuals. The reason correctly identifies a measure with wider reach, although welfare must be assessed carefully rather than reduced to a single average.

A country may produce a celebrated scientist and construct a magnificent capital while many children cannot attend school or receive basic healthcare. Those achievements show talent and resources, but they do not demonstrate that the nation enables most residents to flourish. Access to education, safety, and meaningful opportunity offers a more direct test of what its institutions accomplish.

The claim does not imply that art, science, or leadership are unimportant. A medical discovery can benefit millions, and a novel can deepen public understanding. Their contribution to national greatness is strongest when citizens can participate in and benefit from the institutions behind them. A prize does not excuse exclusion.

The reason also needs qualification. Average income can rise while a vulnerable minority loses rights, and short-term consumption can improve while environmental damage burdens future citizens. General welfare should include distribution, liberty, health, and sustainability.

The claim and reason therefore support one another, but the reason must be given substantive content. Greatness is better tested by how people live, including those without public acclaim, than by the fame of rulers, artists, or scientists alone.

topic: Any leader who is quickly and easily influenced by shifts in popular opinion will accomplish little.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the statement and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the statement might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
essay:
A leader who changes course with every fluctuation in public opinion may struggle to accomplish a long-term goal. I mostly agree with the statement, while distinguishing responsiveness from thoughtless imitation.

A mayor planning a transit system must consider years of construction and financing. If she cancels one route whenever a new poll shows temporary displeasure, workers and residents cannot plan. She should explain the evidence for the design and stay with it through predictable short-term inconvenience. Consistency allows the project to be evaluated on results.

Yet public opinion can reveal a real flaw. If residents with disabilities explain that the stations are inaccessible, a leader should revise the plan. Holding firm merely to appear strong would waste authority and harm the people the system serves. Listening is useful when it adds evidence or exposes neglected interests.

The difference lies in how the leader responds. A poll alone may show anxiety without identifying its cause; meetings, expert review, and transparent reasoning can identify whether a change is warranted. A capable leader can alter a method while preserving the underlying goal of accessible transport.

Popular support matters in a democracy, but its latest movement should not be the sole compass. Leaders accomplish more when they hold clear purposes, invite criticism, and explain why they continue or change a policy. Neither reflexive surrender nor stubbornness is a substitute for judgment.

topic: Government officials should rely on their own judgment rather than unquestioningly carry out the will of the people whom they serve.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the statement and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the statement might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
essay:
Government officials should use judgment rather than simply echo every public demand. I agree with the statement because their responsibilities include evidence, legal rights, and long-term consequences, while public concerns remain essential to good decisions.

Suppose residents ask a health department to close a clinic after an alarming but unverified rumor. An official should investigate and publish the findings before acting. If evidence shows the clinic is safe and urgently needed, closing it merely to follow the loudest voices could harm patients. The official's judgment must be based on more than private confidence: it requires reliable information and an explanation citizens can challenge.

The other danger is treating expertise as permission to dismiss lived experience. If people report that a transit stop is unsafe at night, a planner should not assume a technical map settles the question. Public testimony can reveal conditions missing from official data. Elected officials are accountable to everyone they serve, including those who are not present at a meeting.

The recommendation is strongest when opinion shifts quickly or threatens the rights of a minority. It is least defensible when leaders use “my judgment” to hide self-interest. Consultation, disclosure of evidence, and elections help distinguish principled independence from arrogance.

Officials should neither obey automatically nor rule as if citizens are irrelevant. Their work is to weigh public needs and evidence together and give reasons for the decisions they make.

topic: A nation should require all of its students to study the same national curriculum until they enter college.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the statement and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the statement might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
essay:
A common national curriculum can guarantee access to important knowledge, but requiring every student to study exactly the same material until college would ignore local needs and individual development. I partly disagree with the statement.

Shared instruction in literacy, mathematics, science, and civic history can protect students whose schools might otherwise offer a thin education. A family moving between regions should not find that a child has missed an essential prerequisite. Common standards also give the public a basis for asking whether schools serve students fairly.

Uniformity becomes harmful when it prescribes every text, project, and pace. A coastal community may use local ecology to teach scientific methods; another may study water scarcity. Both can meet the same underlying standard. Students who need additional language support or advanced work may require different routes to mastery. A rigid curriculum could force teachers to move on before one group understands or leave another unchallenged.

National content can also become a political instrument if one authority decides that only a single interpretation of history may be taught. Opportunities to compare sources and question claims are part of a sound civic education.

A better policy establishes a core of knowledge and skills, then gives schools room to adapt examples, offer electives, and support different learners. Equal educational opportunity requires shared expectations, but it does not require identical lessons for every child.

topic: It is primarily in cities that a nation's cultural traditions are generated and preserved.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the statement and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the statement might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
essay:
Cities are important centers of cultural exchange, but I disagree that a nation's traditions are generated and preserved primarily there. Rural communities, smaller towns, and networks that cross both settings also shape a culture.

A city can bring musicians, writers, migrants, and audiences together. New styles may emerge when traditions meet, and museums or archives can preserve records for large numbers of people. These institutions deserve recognition. A performance that develops in a city can later influence an entire nation.

Yet a farming community may maintain a language, seasonal festival, or craft across generations. Some of these practices enter urban stages only after people elsewhere have kept them alive. Treating the city as the origin simply because it has the most visible venues mistakes publicity for creation. Families and local associations are cultural institutions too.

Preservation is not identical to keeping a tradition unchanged. People moving between regions adapt food, music, and stories, sometimes maintaining a connection to home while creating something new. A nation's culture is formed through this movement rather than confined to one type of place.

The claim is useful if it calls attention to the resources cities offer artists and archives. It fails when “primarily” erases the communities whose practices provide much of what urban institutions display. To understand a nation's traditions, we should study cities and the places to which their residents remain connected.

topic: We can learn much more from people whose views we share than from people whose views contradict our own.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the statement and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the statement might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
essay:
Agreement can make collaboration efficient, but disagreement often teaches us what our assumptions leave out. I disagree with the claim that shared views usually yield much more learning.

Suppose a student argues that a city should replace a busy road with a park. Supporters may contribute useful evidence about air quality and public space. A bus driver who worries about rerouted transit adds a question they may not have considered. Addressing that objection could produce a better design with improved bus access, or it could reveal that the original proposal is flawed. Both possibilities are educational.

Opposition can also become unproductive. A person who refuses to listen or attacks motives may make everyone defensive. The benefit comes from relevant reasons and a willingness to revise, not from conflict for its own sake. Likewise, a supportive colleague can point out a mistake without opposing the overall goal. The simple division between agreement and contradiction hides the quality of the exchange.

We need shared purposes to build an idea and differing perspectives to test it. In a classroom, a teacher can encourage students to summarize an objection fairly and compare evidence before deciding. That method lets disagreement deepen understanding instead of becoming a contest.

The strongest learning often occurs when a trusted collaborator is willing to challenge a particular claim. Whether views initially align matters less than whether the conversation exposes new evidence and improves our reasoning.

topic: When old buildings stand on ground that modern planners feel could be better used for modern purposes, modern development should be given precedence over the preservation of historic buildings.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the statement and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the statement might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
essay:
Modern development sometimes deserves priority over preserving an old building, but it should not automatically win because planners see a more profitable use for the land. I disagree with the general rule.

A historic market may anchor a neighborhood's memory and provide affordable space for small traders. Replacing it with offices might raise property values while displacing those businesses. Before demolition, planners should ask whether the structure can be adapted, whether its significance is well documented, and who benefits from the proposed change.

Preservation has limits. An unsafe building with little historical value might occupy land urgently needed for housing or a hospital. Keeping it merely because it is old could impose large costs on residents. A city can record its history, reuse materials, or incorporate part of the site into the new project without freezing every street in place.

The comparison must consider more than projected revenue. Public access, cultural value, safety, and long-term needs belong in the decision. People affected by demolition should have a chance to challenge the planner's assumptions, including the claim that a modern use is necessarily better.

Neither age nor novelty confers automatic priority. Development should proceed when its public benefits are compelling and alternatives are inadequate. Preservation should prevail when the building carries substantial value that cannot be replaced by a newer structure.

topic: Claim: The surest indicator of a great nation must be the achievements of its rulers, artists, or scientists. Reason: Great achievements by a nation's rulers, artists, or scientists will ensure a good life for the majority of that nation's people.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim and the reason on which that claim is based.
essay:
I disagree with the claim that a nation's greatest indicator must be the achievements of rulers, artists, or scientists, and I reject the reason that such achievements will ensure a good life for most people. Excellence at the top does not automatically spread its benefits.

A country can produce a celebrated scientist while many children lack access to basic education. The achievement may be remarkable and eventually useful, but it does not prove that the society has created opportunities for the majority. A ruler may win international praise for a grand project while nearby households lack clean water. Visibility and general welfare measure different things.

The reason becomes persuasive only under conditions it leaves unstated. A medical discovery improves lives widely when it is affordable, distributed, and supported by functioning clinics. A work of art can enrich the public when people can encounter and discuss it. The institutions connecting exceptional work to ordinary lives are crucial; the achievement alone does not guarantee the connection.

Moreover, national greatness should consider those who are not famous. A reliable school system, fair legal process, and public health services reflect sustained work by many people. Their effects may be less dramatic than a prize or monument but more consequential for citizens.

The claim and reason both confuse potential with assurance. Accomplished leaders, artists, and scientists can contribute to a great nation. The strongest evidence of greatness is whether its people, including those outside the spotlight, can live securely and develop their abilities.

topic: Some people claim that you can tell whether a nation is great by looking at the achievements of its rulers, artists, or scientists. Others argue that the surest indicator of a great nation is, in fact, the general welfare of all its people.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss which view more closely aligns with your own position and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should address both of the views presented.
essay:
I align more closely with the view that the general welfare of people is the surest indicator of a nation's greatness. Achievements by rulers, artists, and scientists matter, but their prominence does not tell us how the nation treats most residents.

A country might have a brilliant scientific institute while schools in poorer regions lack teachers. The institute demonstrates talent and may produce discoveries, yet its existence alone does not establish broad opportunity. Measures of health, education, safety, and access to rights provide a fuller picture of what public institutions achieve.

The opposing view captures something real. A scientific breakthrough may save lives elsewhere, and a work of art may give a nation enduring cultural influence. Such accomplishments should be celebrated. But their relevance to national greatness grows when people can benefit from them and participate in the conditions that make future accomplishments possible.

Welfare is also more than a high average income. A prosperous majority can coexist with severe deprivation for a minority. A credible evaluation asks who is excluded and whether today's gains endanger future citizens through debt or environmental damage.

The two views need not treat excellence and welfare as enemies. A nation can cultivate art and science while protecting ordinary life. When forced to choose a measure, however, I would look first at the well-being of its people. Famous achievements are valuable evidence only when examined alongside the lives of those who seldom receive recognition.

topic: The best way to understand the character of a society is to examine the character of the men and women that the society chooses as its heroes or its role models.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim. In developing and supporting your position, be sure to address the most compelling reasons and/or examples that could be used to challenge your position.
essay:
A society's heroes reveal some of its aspirations, but they are not the best single guide to its character. I partly disagree with the statement because public admiration can differ from everyday conduct and from the choices of less powerful groups.

A nation that celebrates a courageous civil rights advocate announces that equality matters. Studying how schools teach that person's life can illuminate values the society wants to pass on. The choice of role models is therefore revealing, particularly when people debate whom to honor.

Yet monuments and official ceremonies can reflect the priorities of authorities more than those of ordinary citizens. A community may praise service publicly while rewarding wealth and status in practice. To understand its character, we should ask whether its institutions treat people fairly, how neighbors help one another, and whose contributions remain invisible.

Heroes can also be contested. One group may see a political leader as a reformer; another may remember the harm the leader caused. That disagreement is itself useful evidence about a society's conflicts and changing ideals. It prevents a simple list of admired figures from standing in for analysis.

Examining role models offers a window into what a society claims to value. Its character becomes clearer when those claims are compared with its laws, opportunities, and ordinary behavior. Admiration matters, but it is only part of the evidence.

topic: All college and university students would benefit from spending at least one semester studying in a foreign country.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the statement and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the statement might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
essay:
A semester in another country can benefit many college students, but I disagree that all would benefit enough to justify treating it as a universal expectation. Its value depends on the program, the student's responsibilities, and the chance to engage meaningfully with the host community.

A student studying public health may learn how another country organizes clinics and understand assumptions she previously took for granted. Living there for months allows more than a tourist's impression. Language practice and friendships can make the learning personal and lasting.

Yet a student caring for a parent at home may face serious harm from leaving for a semester. Another may join a poorly designed exchange that keeps students together in an isolated campus, offering little engagement with local life. Travel alone does not guarantee cultural understanding, and the financial burden can be substantial even when tuition is covered.

Universities should offer scholarships, academic support, and thoughtful partnerships for students who choose to go. They can also create meaningful international collaboration from home through joint projects and visiting scholars. These options are not identical, but they expand access to other perspectives.

The statement is strongest as a call to make study abroad available beyond wealthy students. It overreaches when it assumes every individual will benefit in the same way. The educational quality and fit of the experience matter more than the passport stamp.

topic: Some people claim that a nation's government should preserve its wilderness areas in their natural state. Others argue that these areas should be developed for potential economic gain.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss which view more closely aligns with your own position and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should address both of the views presented.
essay:
I lean toward preserving wilderness areas, although carefully limited development can be justified where a community has urgent needs. The first view recognizes the irreversible loss that development can cause; the second rightly asks whether protected land can also support livelihoods.

A forest may regulate water, provide habitat, and offer a place for future generations to study and enjoy. Once roads and mines fragment it, restoration may be impossible. If officials look only at immediate revenue, they may underestimate long-term ecological and economic value. Preservation can also protect communities that rely on the forest rather than merely serve visitors.

Yet a blanket ban can impose costs on residents who lack electricity, transport, or work. A proposed road might connect isolated villages to hospitals. Officials should examine routes that avoid the most fragile areas, consult residents, and assess whether the promised benefits will actually reach them. Development should not be approved simply because a company can profit from extraction.

The choice is not always total preservation or unrestricted construction. Protected cores, limited access, and investment in alternatives can sometimes meet both aims. In other cases, the ecological harm is too great and the project should be rejected.

I favor a presumption of preservation because wilderness cannot easily be recreated. That presumption may yield to a compelling public need after transparent review, but not to a vague promise of economic gain.

topic: In most professions and academic fields, imagination is more important than knowledge.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim. In developing and supporting your position, be sure to address the most compelling reasons and/or examples that could be used to challenge your position.
essay:
Imagination allows professionals to propose alternatives, while knowledge lets them judge whether those alternatives can work. I disagree that imagination is generally more important than knowledge across most fields, although breakthroughs often require both.

A physician may imagine a new treatment after noticing that patients respond differently to an established drug. The hypothesis is valuable, but knowledge of physiology and clinical testing is necessary to distinguish a genuine effect from coincidence and to protect patients. An untested creative guess is not yet a medical advance.

In architecture, knowledge of materials and safety codes similarly constrains a design. Those constraints can stimulate rather than suppress imagination: a designer might find an elegant way to use less energy while making a building accessible. Knowing what earlier designs achieved also prevents the reinvention of failed solutions.

The claim is more persuasive when a field has become complacent. Experts can assume a problem has only one acceptable solution, and an imaginative outsider may expose that assumption. But the outsider's idea gains value when it is developed and tested against reality. Knowledge is not merely a stock of facts; it includes ways to evaluate a proposal.

No universal ranking will fit every task. Routine practice may depend more heavily on established knowledge, while a novel challenge may demand unusual imagination. Across both cases, the strongest work joins inventive possibilities with disciplined understanding.

topic: The surest indicator of a great nation is not the achievements of its rulers, artists, or scientists, but the general well-being of all its people.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim. In developing and supporting your position, be sure to address the most compelling reasons and/or examples that could be used to challenge your position.
essay:
I agree that the well-being of a nation's people is a surer indicator of its greatness than the accomplishments of its most celebrated figures. A nation is a shared political community, so its institutions should be judged by the lives they make possible for ordinary citizens.

A ruler may build a magnificent capital while rural households lack safe water. Visitors could admire the architecture without seeing the deprivation that helped pay for it. A scientist may win a major prize while talented children from poorer families cannot enter a laboratory. Individual brilliance is real, but it does not by itself show that opportunity is broadly available.

This does not make art or discovery unimportant. A composer can give people a shared cultural language, and a medical advance can improve health far beyond national borders. These achievements strengthen a nation's claim to greatness when they are supported by and contribute to a society in which many can flourish.

Well-being requires more than an average income figure. It includes health, education, rights, and security, and it must be examined across regions and groups. A prosperous majority should not conceal the exclusion of a minority. The ability to sustain those benefits for future generations also matters.

The statement wisely directs attention away from a few visible names. We should honor exceptional work, but assess national greatness by whether the wider population can live with dignity and develop its potential.

topic: Some people argue that successful leaders in government, industry, or other fields must be highly competitive. Other people claim that in order to be successful, a leader must be willing and able to cooperate with others.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss which view more closely aligns with your own position and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should address both of the views presented.
essay:
I align more closely with the view that successful leaders must cooperate with others. Competition can sharpen a goal, but leadership usually requires people with different skills and interests to work toward it.

A company director may compete fiercely with other firms, yet she cannot design, manufacture, and support a product alone. She must listen to engineers, negotiate with suppliers, and make room for colleagues to correct her mistakes. If she treats every internal disagreement as a contest to win, information may stop reaching her.

The competitive view has merit. An elected leader may need to challenge an entrenched system or defend a policy against strong opposition. The desire to achieve results can prevent complacency. But even a reformer needs a coalition to pass a law and people willing to implement it. Victory in a debate is not the same as lasting change.

Cooperation should not mean avoiding difficult choices or surrendering principles. A leader can negotiate methods while being clear about the aim. The most useful competitive energy is directed toward solving a problem, not defeating colleagues for status.

The two qualities can coexist, but cooperation is the more fundamental measure of leadership. People who cannot bring others into a common effort may win attention and still fail to accomplish the work.

topic: College students should base their choice of a field of study on the availability of jobs in that field.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the recommendation and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, describe specific circumstances in which adopting the recommendation would or would not be advantageous and explain how these examples shape your position.
essay:
The availability of jobs should inform a student's choice of field, but it should not determine it alone. I partly disagree with the recommendation because today's labor market is uncertain and long-term success also depends on aptitude and interest.

A student attracted to computer science may see many openings and decide to study it. That is sensible if she enjoys solving programming problems and understands the work. If she dislikes the subject, however, a vacancy count will not help her persist through demanding courses or a career. Advisers should help students test a field through projects or internships, not merely cite employment data.

Financial circumstances matter. Someone who must borrow heavily has a strong reason to compare tuition, likely earnings, and alternative credentials. Ignoring such evidence would be irresponsible. Yet job markets can change before graduation, so broad skills and the capacity to keep learning are also valuable.

The recommendation is advantageous when it prevents an uninformed, costly decision. It is less useful when it pushes every student into a temporarily popular field regardless of fit. Students should weigh opportunities alongside their abilities, interests, costs, and a realistic plan for applying what they learn.

topic: Some people believe that corporations have a responsibility to promote the well- being of the societies and environments in which they operate. Others believe that the only responsibility of corporations, provided they operate within the law, is to make as much money as possible.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss which view more closely aligns with your own position and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should address both of the views presented.
essay:
I align more closely with the view that corporations have responsibilities to the societies and environments in which they operate. Compliance with the law and the pursuit of profit are necessary parts of business, but the second view treats legal minimums as though they capture every effect a firm has on others.

A factory may meet current emissions rules while releasing pollution that residents can plausibly link to health problems. If managers wait for a lawsuit before improving filters, they transfer costs to neighbors who did not choose to bear them. A responsible company should investigate, disclose evidence, and reduce avoidable harm.

The profit-focused view makes a useful objection: executives cannot spend without limit on every worthy cause, and a business that fails financially cannot employ people for long. Responsibilities need to be connected to the firm's activities and weighed against its ability to operate. A small shop, for example, cannot fund every public service, though it can pay workers fairly and dispose of waste safely.

Law remains crucial for setting common standards so responsible firms are not punished for acting alone. But rules may lag behind new technologies or local harms. Companies make choices in that gap, and those choices have moral consequences.

Profit is a legitimate measure of whether a firm can sustain itself. It is not a complete measure of its contribution. A corporation should be judged by the value it creates and by the costs it imposes on workers, communities, and the environment.

topic: Claim: Researchers should not limit their investigations to only those areas in which they expect to discover something that has an immediate, practical application. Reason: It is impossible to predict the outcome of a line of research with any certainty.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim and the reason on which that claim is based.
essay:
I agree with the claim that researchers should not confine themselves to work with immediate practical applications. The reason is persuasive: the outcomes of an inquiry cannot be predicted with certainty. It is not the only reason, because knowledge can also be worth pursuing before a use is identified.

A scientist investigating an obscure property of light may have no device to promise a funder. Years later, the finding could support imaging or communication tools. Demanding a near-term product would prevent the early work. Even a project that never yields a commercial application can improve methods or explain a natural phenomenon.

The reason should not be overstated. Researchers can sometimes make reasonable forecasts about usefulness, and public agencies facing urgent health problems should fund applied work. Unpredictability is a reason to maintain a portfolio of projects, not to ignore evidence about likely benefits. Grants can still be assessed for sound methods, scientific significance, and safety.

An uncertain outcome also differs from an uncontrolled hazard. A dangerous experiment involving pathogens needs stringent review even if the question is valuable. The claim protects freedom to ask questions, not freedom to expose others to avoidable risk.

The reason supports the claim because discovery often opens paths no one foresaw. A balanced research system finances both immediate needs and careful basic inquiry, allowing future applications to emerge without requiring them to be specified in advance.

topic: Some people believe that our ever-increasing use of technology significantly reduces our opportunities for human interaction. Other people believe that technology provides us with new and better ways to communicate and connect with one another.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss which view more closely aligns with your own position and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should address both of the views presented.
essay:
I align more closely with the view that technology offers new ways to connect people, although the opposing view identifies a genuine cost when digital contact displaces attention to those nearby.

A student living far from her family can speak with them regularly by video. People with rare illnesses can find peers who understand their experience and exchange practical advice. Without these tools, distance or isolation might prevent those relationships. Technology expands the set of people with whom meaningful contact is possible.

Yet a family member who repeatedly checks messages during dinner may be physically present and emotionally absent. Online platforms can encourage brief reactions instead of sustained conversation. The problem is not that mediated interaction is inherently unreal; it is that attention is limited. A new connection can become valuable or can crowd out one already worth maintaining.

The two views can both describe different uses of the same device. An exchange of supportive messages during a crisis may strengthen a relationship, while endless scrolling through strangers' posts may leave a person lonely. Design choices matter too: platforms can reward compulsive engagement or make intentional communication easier.

I choose the second view because technology's capacity to cross distance is a substantial gain. To realize it, people need habits and tools that protect attention. The quality of interaction, rather than the mere presence of a screen, should guide the judgment.

topic: Claim: Knowing about the past cannot help people to make important decisions today. Reason: The world today is significantly more complex than it was even in the relatively recent past.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim and the reason on which that claim is based.
essay:
I disagree with both the claim that the past cannot help present decisions and the reason that today's greater complexity makes historical knowledge irrelevant. Complexity calls for careful comparison, not historical amnesia.

A government preparing for a disease outbreak can study how earlier campaigns communicated uncertainty and distributed supplies. Today's travel patterns and medical tools differ, so an old plan cannot simply be copied. Yet records of which communities were excluded or which messages earned trust can guide questions officials should ask now. Historical evidence helps identify a risk even when it does not supply an exact answer.

The reason captures a limitation. A policy that worked for a small region decades ago may fail in a connected modern economy. Responsible decision makers must identify which causes are similar and which have changed. But if the world is complex, a wider range of evidence becomes more useful. Ignoring earlier cases would remove one source of that evidence.

History also shows the origins of current institutions. A city debating housing rules can learn why older zoning decisions produced unequal access. Without that account, today's problem may appear natural or inevitable.

The claim confuses imperfect analogy with uselessness. We should neither romanticize past solutions nor dismiss past experience. Studied critically, history makes present choices more informed by revealing consequences, assumptions, and changes over time.

topic: Claim: Knowing about the past cannot help people to make important decisions today. Reason: We are not able to make connections between current events and past events until we have some distance from both.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim and the reason on which that claim is based.
essay:
I disagree that knowledge of the past cannot help current decisions, and I do not think the reason establishes it. We may need distance to assess the full meaning of an event, but we can still draw cautious lessons before every consequence is known.

Suppose a city is rebuilding after a flood. Records from earlier floods can reveal which evacuation routes failed and whose warnings were ignored. Officials need not know the final historical interpretation of either event to use that practical information. They should check whether roads, population, and weather conditions have changed before applying it.

The reason does identify a danger in quick analogies. A leader may declare that a new conflict is “just like” a famous one and overlook crucial differences. Distance can make additional documents available and reduce the emotional pressure to choose a simple story. That is an argument for humility, not for abandoning historical comparison.

Present events are also understood through earlier institutions and choices. A debate over housing cannot be evaluated well without knowing how existing neighborhoods and regulations developed. Some causal links are available now even if later historians will revise them.

The claim demands a certainty that history need not provide. Past cases can suggest questions, warn of foreseeable harms, and expose assumptions. Decision makers should state the limits of each analogy, update it with current evidence, and act without pretending to have a perfect view of either era.

topic: Educational institutions should actively encourage their students to choose fields of study that will prepare them for lucrative careers.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss your views on the policy and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider the possible consequences of implementing the policy and explain how these consequences shape your position.
essay:
Colleges should help students understand lucrative career paths, but they should not steer every student toward them as though salary were the main purpose of education. I partly disagree with the statement.

A student from a low-income family may benefit from learning which qualifications lead to stable, well-paid work. Clear information about costs, salaries, and internships can expand choices that the student did not know existed. Avoiding the subject of earnings in the name of intellectual freedom could leave some graduates with debt they cannot manage.

Yet salary alone does not predict a good match. A student who excels at teaching and wants to work with children may find sustained purpose there even if another field pays more. Pushing her into an occupation she dislikes could lead to poor work and eventual departure. Labor markets also change during the years a degree takes to complete.

An institution should disclose outcomes honestly and allow students to explore interests through courses and practical experience. It can show how a field connects to several careers and help students develop transferable skills. This is guidance, not an instruction to maximize income.

Lucrative work is a legitimate goal, especially when financial security is urgent. Educational institutions serve students best when they help each person weigh that goal against aptitude, purpose, debt, and the realities of the profession.

topic: Educational institutions should actively encourage their students to choose fields of study in which jobs are plentiful.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim. In developing and supporting your position, be sure to address the most compelling reasons and/or examples that could be used to challenge your position.
essay:
Educational institutions should make students aware of fields with plentiful jobs, but actively encouraging everyone toward those fields risks confusing current demand with long-term fit. I partly disagree with the statement.

A school might see many openings in healthcare and invite students to explore nursing through classes and placements. For a student who enjoys patient care, that information can reveal a promising route. Another student may find the clinical work distressing and serve society better in a different field. Job availability cannot replace experience of the work.

The number of vacancies also changes. If many institutions respond to one shortage at once, graduates may face a different market several years later. A course that teaches adaptable reasoning and practical skills may provide more security than a narrow bet on today's figures. Students should compare outcomes but understand the uncertainty in forecasts.

The contrary concern is real: institutions that charge high fees while refusing to discuss employment leave students vulnerable. Advisers should offer transparent data, internships, and plans for applying a chosen subject. They should not dismiss the importance of earning a living.

The best encouragement helps students find where their abilities and interests meet credible opportunities. It informs a decision without making a temporary labor-market signal the institution's command.

topic: Educational institutions have a responsibility to dissuade students from pursuing fields of study in which they are unlikely to succeed.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the statement and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the statement might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
essay:
Institutions should be honest when a student is struggling in a chosen field, but they should not assume they can reliably decide in advance who is unlikely to succeed. I partly disagree with the duty to dissuade.

A student who wants to study physics but has weak algebra skills may need tutoring and more time. Advising a change of major immediately could turn an educational gap into a permanent judgment about ability. A school has a responsibility to offer support and clear milestones before concluding that the route is impractical.

Honesty becomes essential when failure has significant costs. If a trainee repeatedly cannot meet clinical safety standards after meaningful instruction, an adviser should explain the evidence and discuss alternative roles. Concealing the problem would waste the student's money and potentially put patients at risk. The discussion should concern demonstrated performance, not background or stereotypes.

Students retain the right to choose a difficult path with their eyes open. Institutions can explain requirements, probabilities, and options for preparation without issuing a verdict on a person's future. Sometimes dissuasion is appropriate, but it should follow fair assessment and opportunities to improve.

A responsible adviser replaces a vague prediction with specific evidence and choices. The institution's primary duty is to help students learn and make informed decisions, including decisions to change direction when the evidence warrants it.

topic: Some people believe that competition for high grades motivates students to excel in the classroom. Others believe that such competition seriously limits the quality of real learning.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss which view more closely aligns with your own position and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should address both of the views presented.
essay:
I align more closely with the view that competition for high grades can limit real learning, though the first view correctly observes that evaluation can motivate effort.

A student may practice harder when an exam provides a clear target and recognizes progress. Grades can reveal which skills need attention and help schools maintain standards. A complete absence of feedback can leave learners uncertain about their work.

But when every classmate is a rival, students may hide confusion, choose easy courses to protect an average, or memorize likely answers instead of exploring the subject. A biology student who knows definitions but cannot design an experiment has learned to perform for a test rather than reason scientifically. The costs grow when one ranking dominates college admission or family approval.

The solution is not to abolish assessment. Teachers can offer feedback on drafts, opportunities to revise, and questions that require explanation and application. Students can then pursue demanding work without treating every mistake as a permanent loss. Grades may still summarize achievement, but they should not be the only reason to study.

The first view identifies a useful incentive in limited circumstances. The second better describes what happens when competition becomes the organizing principle of the classroom. Genuine excellence includes curiosity, cooperation, and the ability to improve after an error.

topic: Claim: Major policy decisions should always be left to politicians and other government experts. Reason: Politicians and other government experts are more informed and thus have better judgment and perspective than do members of the general public.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim and the reason on which that claim is based.
essay:
I disagree with the claim that major policy decisions should always be left to politicians and experts. The reason is partly true: specialists often know more about a technical issue. It does not follow that they have better judgment about every value and burden involved.

An epidemiologist can estimate how a disease spreads, while public-health officials can compare possible interventions. Their knowledge is essential. But a decision to close schools also affects families, workers, and children in ways a disease model may not measure. People living with those consequences can provide evidence and contest which sacrifices are acceptable.

Elected politicians have a mandate to weigh competing needs, but they can also make mistakes or face conflicts of interest. Public hearings, journalism, and citizen groups provide checks. A popular demand can be misinformed, so participation should include access to credible evidence and a clear explanation of tradeoffs. It need not mean that a poll determines every technical detail.

The reason conflates information with authority. Experts can explain likely outcomes; citizens have standing to discuss the goals a policy should serve and the distribution of its costs. Representatives should listen to both and make decisions they can defend publicly.

The claim would exclude the people government exists to serve. Major decisions require expertise and accountable institutions, but their legitimacy and quality improve when affected communities can question assumptions and shape the choice.

topic: Some people believe that universities should require every student to take a variety of courses outside the student's field of study. Others believe that universities should not force students to take any courses other than those that will help prepare them for jobs in their chosen fields.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss which view more closely aligns with your own position and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should address both of the views presented.
essay:
I align more closely with the view that universities should require some courses outside a major. The opposing view rightly worries about cost and career preparation, but a narrow curriculum can leave graduates unable to understand the contexts in which their specialized skills will be used.

An engineering student may design a water system more responsibly after studying public policy and learning how fees affect poor households. A literature student who takes statistics can better assess numerical claims in research or journalism. Such courses are not distractions from work; they can make professional judgment stronger.

The opposing view is most persuasive for students facing high tuition or a tightly regulated professional program. A large set of unrelated requirements could delay graduation without offering meaningful breadth. Universities should keep the requirement modest, allow students to choose among serious courses, and show how those courses connect to wider reasoning and citizenship.

Job preparation is not confined to major courses. Graduates work with people who have different expertise and must evaluate claims outside their specialty. At the same time, breadth should not crowd out the depth needed to perform a profession competently.

I therefore favor a balanced curriculum rather than either extreme. A university should make room for specialized training and require students to engage thoughtfully with at least some ideas beyond it.

topic: It is more harmful to compromise one's own beliefs than to adhere to them.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the statement and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the statement might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
essay:
Compromising a belief can be harmful when it means abandoning a fundamental principle for convenience. But adhering to every belief regardless of new evidence can be worse. I disagree with the absolute comparison.

A public official who believes all citizens deserve equal treatment should not trade that commitment away merely to secure an easier political deal. In this case, compromise could directly harm people whose rights depend on the principle. Integrity requires explaining the boundary and seeking other ways to advance a policy.

Yet many beliefs concern facts or methods rather than core values. A doctor who once favored a treatment should change her view when reliable trials show it is ineffective. Refusing to compromise because the view feels personal would harm patients. A leader can likewise preserve a goal, such as safer streets, while revising a flawed plan after residents explain its effects.

Even a principled person should ask whether a particular belief is well founded and what adherence costs others. Changing one's mind after serious inquiry is not necessarily weakness. Conversely, a person who yields to pressure without examining the reasons may lose trust in their own judgment.

The harm depends on what is being compromised and why. People should hold firmly to defensible ethical commitments while remaining open to evidence and better methods. Neither stubbornness nor agreement is virtuous on its own.

topic: Claim: Colleges and universities should specify all required courses and eliminate elective courses in order to provide clear guidance for students. Reason: College students — like people in general — prefer to follow directions rather than make their own decisions.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim and the reason on which that claim is based.
essay:
I disagree with the claim that colleges should eliminate electives and with the reason that students' supposed preference for direction justifies doing so. Guidance can help students choose, but replacing choice entirely would weaken education.

A first-year student may feel overwhelmed by hundreds of courses. Advisers can explain requirements, show possible paths, and help the student test an interest through an introductory class. That responds to uncertainty without assuming the student cannot decide. Learning to make an informed choice is itself preparation for life after college.

Electives can reveal a valuable connection. A computer science student who takes a linguistics course may discover a question about language technology that becomes a research project. If every course were specified in advance, such exploration would depend on luck outside the university. A rigid program may also fail to adapt to new fields.

Some required courses are necessary. A nursing student must master safety and clinical foundations before treating patients. Clear sequences can prevent gaps and delays. But the existence of essential prerequisites does not establish that all remaining learning should be prescribed.

The reason is a broad psychological claim without sufficient support. Students may ask for advice and still value agency. Colleges should provide a coherent core, transparent pathways, and strong advising while preserving meaningful electives. That approach offers direction and teaches responsible choice rather than treating adults as incapable of it.

topic: No field of study can advance significantly unless it incorporates knowledge and experience from outside that field.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the statement and explain your reasoning for the position you take.
