In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the statement might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
essay:
Fields often advance by borrowing methods or ideas from elsewhere, but “no field” and “impossible” make the claim too absolute. I largely agree that outside knowledge is a powerful source of progress, while recognizing that important work can also occur within a discipline's own questions.

Medical researchers have gained from statistics and computer science, which help them analyze large collections of observations. Ecologists use economic ideas when evaluating incentives that affect conservation. These exchanges can reveal patterns a single discipline would miss. They also force specialists to explain their assumptions to people trained differently.

Yet a mathematician can prove a new result by working deeply with concepts developed within mathematics. The achievement may be significant before an external application or borrowed method appears. External influence is not a requirement that can be demonstrated for every contribution. Excessive emphasis on fashionable interdisciplinary labels could also draw attention from foundational problems.

The key is openness rather than a quota of outside material. Researchers should understand their own methods well enough to know when another field offers a useful tool and when an analogy is superficial. Collaboration works best when participants can test ideas against the standards of the problem at hand.

Most fields benefit greatly from crossing boundaries, especially when complex problems span social and technical systems. But significant progress can arise from both internal development and informed exchange. The statement captures a strong tendency, not a logical necessity.

topic: True success can be measured primarily in terms of the goals one sets for oneself.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the statement and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the statement might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
essay:
The goals people choose are central to judging success, but they are not a complete measure. I partly agree with the statement because a private objective gives an achievement meaning, while the consequences for others also matter.

A musician who wants to perform confidently at a local concert may consider the evening a success even without fame. Comparing her with a world-renowned performer would miss the work she set out to do. Goals help distinguish genuine progress from status imposed by others.

Yet a person can set a goal that is too easy or harmful. A manager might aim only to cut labor costs and declare success after laying off workers, while leaving a business unable to serve customers. Meeting the chosen target would not settle whether the outcome was admirable. Goals should be assessed for ambition, fairness, and their effects.

Circumstances matter too. Someone caring for an ill relative may fall short of a career target yet accomplish something deeply valuable. A rigid comparison with an earlier plan would understate that success. People should be able to revise goals as responsibilities and knowledge change.

Self-chosen aims are a useful starting point because they honor individual purpose. True success also requires honest reflection on the quality of those aims, the means used, and the lives affected along the way.

topic: The general welfare of a nation's people is a better indication of that nation's greatness than are the achievements of its rulers, artists, or scientists.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim. In developing and supporting your position, be sure to address the most compelling reasons and/or examples that could be used to challenge your position.
essay:
I agree that the well-being of a nation's people is a surer indicator of its greatness than the accomplishments of its most celebrated figures. A nation is a shared political community, so its institutions should be judged by the lives they make possible for ordinary citizens.

A ruler may build a magnificent capital while rural households lack safe water. Visitors could admire the architecture without seeing the deprivation that helped pay for it. A scientist may win a major prize while talented children from poorer families cannot enter a laboratory. Individual brilliance is real, but it does not by itself show that opportunity is broadly available.

This does not make art or discovery unimportant. A composer can give people a shared cultural language, and a medical advance can improve health far beyond national borders. These achievements strengthen a nation's claim to greatness when they are supported by and contribute to a society in which many can flourish.

Well-being requires more than an average income figure. It includes health, education, rights, and security, and it must be examined across regions and groups. A prosperous majority should not conceal the exclusion of a minority. The ability to sustain those benefits for future generations also matters.

The statement wisely directs attention away from a few visible names. We should honor exceptional work, but assess national greatness by whether the wider population can live with dignity and develop its potential.

topic: The best test of an argument is the argument's ability to convince someone with an opposing viewpoint.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the statement and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the statement might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
essay:
An argument's ability to persuade an opponent is a valuable test, but it is not always the best test. I partly disagree because a sound argument may fail to convince someone who will not consider evidence, while a weak one may persuade through rhetoric.

In a town debate about water safety, residents who distrust officials may ask hard questions that expose gaps in a proposed plan. If the officials can answer those objections with measurements and clear safeguards, the argument grows stronger. Engagement with an opposing view can reveal hidden assumptions and make reasoning more precise.

Yet an opponent might reject every reliable test because accepting the result threatens a personal interest. Failure to win that person over does not make the evidence false. Conversely, a charismatic speaker might convince an audience with a moving story that represents an unusual case as typical. Persuasion alone would reward style over accuracy.

A better evaluation asks whether premises are supported, whether the conclusion follows, and whether serious counterexamples have been addressed. Persuading a thoughtful critic can provide evidence of these qualities, but the critic's reaction is one indicator among others.

Arguments should be clear enough to be examined by people who disagree. Their ultimate standard is not applause or conversion, however; it is whether their reasoning withstands fair scrutiny.

topic: The effectiveness of a country's leaders is best measured by examining the well- being of that country's citizens.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the statement and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the statement might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
essay:
A leader's effectiveness should be judged substantially by how citizens fare. I agree with the statement, provided that well-being is measured over time and that leaders are held responsible only for effects they could reasonably influence.

A mayor who improves access to clean water and reliable clinics has produced results that matter more than a polished speech or a high approval rating. Looking at infant health, service availability, and whether poorer districts benefit can reveal whether policy reached people. Such outcomes are a useful check on a leader's promises.

Yet a sudden drought or global recession may harm citizens despite competent action. Conversely, a leader can inherit favorable conditions and claim credit for prosperity already underway. Evaluation should compare choices with realistic alternatives and consider the resources and constraints the leader faced. It should also watch for policies that improve a short-term statistic while creating future debt or environmental damage.

Well-being includes more than income. Safety, rights, education, and the ability to participate in public life all matter. A government that raises average output while silencing criticism cannot claim unqualified success from the economic figure alone.

Citizen welfare is the best starting point because leadership is a public responsibility, not a personal performance. A careful judgment links outcomes to decisions, considers distribution and duration, and asks whether citizens are better able to lead secure and meaningful lives.

topic: Nations should pass laws to preserve any remaining wilderness areas in their natural state.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim. In developing and supporting your position, be sure to address the most compelling reasons and/or examples that could be used to challenge your position.
essay:
Laws can protect wilderness from irreversible loss, and I support strong preservation in many cases. I do not support a rule that every remaining wilderness area must be frozen in precisely its present state without considering local needs.

A forest can support wildlife, regulate water, and preserve a place for future generations to study and enjoy. Once roads and mines fragment it, restoration may be difficult or impossible. Clear legal protection can prevent a series of small approvals from destroying the whole ecosystem before the public recognizes what is happening.

But a community might need a carefully located road to reach a hospital. Legislators should examine alternative routes and designs rather than declare that no use can ever be permitted. They should also consult people who live near or depend on the land; protection should not become an excuse to exclude them from decisions about their home.

The law can designate highly sensitive cores, regulate surrounding areas, and require rigorous review of exceptions. This approach is not a license for routine development. The presumption should favor preservation when ecological harm is uncertain and irreversible.

A national commitment to wilderness is valuable because immediate profit often dominates longer-term benefits. Its strength lies in durable, well-designed protections, not a blanket phrase that ignores differences among places and needs.

topic: In any field — business, politics, education, government — those in power should be required to step down after five years.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss your views on the policy and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider the possible consequences of implementing the policy and explain how these consequences shape your position.
essay:
A mandatory five-year turnover rule might prevent some leaders from entrenching themselves, but applying it in every field would sacrifice useful experience without guaranteeing renewal. I disagree with the universal requirement.

In government, term limits can restrain officials who use their office to weaken competition. Yet voters may also have good reasons to retain a representative who remains effective and accountable. The case for a particular limit depends on the office and the quality of elections and oversight, not merely on a number.

An academic director may need more than five years to build a research program. A failing business might need new management after only two. In both settings, a fixed deadline tells us little about performance. Boards, colleagues, and the public should have ways to challenge a leader's decisions and plan for succession before a crisis occurs.

The desire for fresh ideas is legitimate. Institutions can rotate responsibilities, mentor successors, and invite outside criticism even when a leader stays. Turnover should be possible and sometimes compulsory after abuse, but it is not automatically beneficial on a universal schedule.

Five years may be a reasonable limit for a particular role. It is a poor rule for all positions of power. Accountability and the capacity to renew an institution matter more than identical terms across unrelated fields.

topic: Some people claim that the goal of politics should be the pursuit of an ideal. Others argue that the goal should be finding common ground and reaching reasonable consensus.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss which view more closely aligns with your own position and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should address both of the views presented.
essay:
I lean toward the view that politics should seek common ground and reasonable consensus, while accepting that ideals give compromise its direction. The first view can inspire reform; the second offers a way to make it durable in a society whose members disagree.

Consider a legislature trying to reduce pollution. An ideal of clean air may justify ambitious standards. Workers and low-income households may nevertheless fear the immediate cost of a rapid transition. A policy that phases in requirements and supports affected families could produce real improvement where an uncompromising proposal would fail.

The danger in consensus is that a powerful majority can agree to sacrifice the rights of others. A bargain that excludes a minority from voting is not reasonable because several parties signed it. Politicians need principles that set boundaries on acceptable compromise. They should explain those boundaries rather than use the language of pragmatism to conceal abandonment.

The ideal-focused view has its own risk. A politician who rejects every partial gain may leave an unjust system intact. Practical agreements can create a foundation for later change, provided they move toward the goal and do not entrench a new harm.

The two views are most useful together, but when choosing a daily aim for politics, I favor principled consensus. It requires leaders to listen, identify attainable improvements, and be candid about what they will not trade away.

topic: The best way to solve environmental problems caused by consumer-generated waste is for towns and cities to impose strict limits on the amount of trash they will accept from each household.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim. In developing and supporting your position, be sure to address the most compelling reasons and/or examples that could be used to challenge your position.
essay:
Limits on household trash might reduce waste, but they are not the best general solution to consumer-generated environmental problems. I disagree with the proposal because disposal is only the last stage of a system shaped by packaging, product design, and access to recycling.

A town that accepts only one small bin per household may prompt some residents to buy less and sort materials carefully. Others may have no practical alternative to heavily packaged goods, and some may dump excess waste illegally. The same limit could affect a large family much more than a single resident. Without convenient collection and fair allowances, the rule may move the waste rather than reduce it.

Manufacturers can often change the amount of material before it enters a household. Refillable containers, repairable products, and packaging standards may prevent waste at its source. Municipalities can support composting and reliable recycling, while charging for excess disposal after a reasonable basic amount. Such policies share responsibility more fairly.

Strict limits may be useful where landfill space is scarce and alternatives already exist. They are less effective when residents lack those alternatives or when enforcement causes illegal dumping. Officials should measure total waste, not merely the volume accepted by the town.

The best approach addresses production, consumption, and disposal together. Household limits can be one tool, but making them the central answer asks residents to solve a problem they did not create alone.

topic: We learn our most valuable lessons in life from struggling with our limitations rather than from enjoying our successes.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim. In developing and supporting your position, be sure to address the most compelling reasons and/or examples that could be used to challenge your position.
essay:
Struggling with a limitation can teach persistence and ingenuity, but success can also teach valuable lessons. I disagree that the former is generally the source of our most valuable learning.

A student who fails an examination may discover that memorizing formulas without understanding their use is ineffective. Revising the study method and asking for feedback can turn the setback into real progress. Without reflection, however, repeated failure may simply discourage the student. Hardship does not teach automatically.

Success has information too. A team that launches a useful community project can study why residents participated and which methods worked. That knowledge may help it sustain and expand the effort. Celebrating an outcome without analysis misses the lesson, just as dwelling on a failure without changing course does.

The claim is strongest when comfort prevents people from testing their abilities. A person who never attempts a difficult task may not discover what preparation is needed. But deliberately seeking hardship for its own sake is unnecessary; many lessons can be learned through observation, practice, and careful review of outcomes.

The most valuable teacher is reflection supported by evidence. Limitations expose gaps, while successes reveal effective choices and opportunities. People grow when they examine both honestly rather than assuming that pain is intrinsically more instructive than achievement.

topic: Claim: While boredom is often expressed with a sense of self-satisfaction, it should really be a source of embarrassment. Reason: Boredom arises from a lack of imagination and self-motivation.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim and the reason on which that claim is based.
essay:
I disagree that boredom should usually be embarrassing, and the reason that it always reflects a lack of imagination or motivation is too narrow. Boredom can be a signal about a person's habits, but it can also arise from circumstances outside personal control.

A student who scrolls through entertainment for hours and finds nothing satisfying might benefit from trying a difficult project or spending time with friends. In that case, boredom can prompt more intentional choices. Shame, however, is unlikely to teach the student what kind of activity is meaningful.

Consider a worker assigned repetitive tasks with no opportunity to learn or vary the routine. The worker may be imaginative and motivated yet bored by the job's design. An institution could respond with training or more varied responsibilities instead of treating the feeling as a personal defect. Illness, exhaustion, and isolation can also make engagement difficult.

The claim associates boredom with self-satisfaction, but some people are distressed by it; others use a quiet interval to reflect and create. Whether it is useful depends on its cause and the response it inspires. A universal moral judgment hides that variation.

The reason does not establish the claim. We should ask what boredom reveals about attention, opportunity, and purpose, then make changes where possible. Embarrassment may add a burden without improving imagination or motivation.

topic: Some people believe that the most important qualities of an effective teacher are understanding and empathy. Others believe that it is more important for teachers to be rigorous and demanding in their expectations for students.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss which view more closely aligns with your own position and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should address both of the views presented.
essay:
I align more closely with the view that effective teaching requires understanding and empathy, while recognizing that students also need demanding expectations. Empathy helps a teacher know how to set and support those expectations rather than simply lowering them.

A mathematics teacher who notices a student repeatedly making the same error might ask the student to explain the method. The response may reveal a misunderstood concept rather than laziness. Patient feedback and targeted practice can help the student meet a rigorous standard. A teacher who offers sympathy without correcting the error would fail, but so would one who imposes a penalty without diagnosis.

The opposing view rightly resists a classroom in which learners are never challenged. A teacher should assign difficult texts, insist on evidence, and tell students when work needs revision. Yet demanding work is most productive when students trust that mistakes can lead to learning rather than humiliation. Understanding does not mean approving every excuse; it means responding to the actual obstacle.

Expectations should remain high across backgrounds. Empathy can expose unequal resources and guide fair support, while rigor ensures that support leads to genuine mastery. Neither quality works well as a substitute for the other.

I choose the first view because understanding students is the foundation for effective challenge. The best teachers use that understanding to ask more of learners and to show them how to succeed.

topic: Claim: Though often considered an objective pursuit, learning about the historical past requires creativity. Reason: Because we can never know the past directly, we must reconstruct it by imaginatively interpreting historical accounts, documents, and artifacts.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim and the reason on which the claim is based.
essay:
I agree that reconstructing the past requires creativity, and the reason explains why: historians cannot observe most past events directly. Yet imagination must be disciplined by surviving evidence, or it becomes fiction presented as history.

Suppose a historian studies a workers' protest using newspaper reports, letters, and wage records. Each source offers a partial view. The historian must imagine how events might connect, ask why witnesses disagree, and develop an account that makes sense of the evidence. No document simply hands over a complete narrative.

The reason can be misunderstood. Our distance from the past does not give historians permission to invent motives or incidents without support. A plausible interpretation should identify its sources, acknowledge missing voices, and remain open to correction when new records appear. Creativity is valuable in forming questions and considering alternative explanations, not in replacing evidence.

The claim also applies to choosing what to examine. A researcher may connect an ordinary household object with trade records to reveal a history that official speeches ignored. That insight requires both inventive attention and careful verification.

Historical study is therefore neither mechanical transcription nor unconstrained storytelling. Because we cannot know the past directly, we interpret traces of it. The quality of that interpretation depends on how imaginative possibilities are tested against what the record can and cannot sustain.

topic: Claim: No act is done purely for the benefit of others. Reason: All actions — even those that seem to be done for other people — are based on self-interest.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim and the reason on which that claim is based.
essay:
I disagree with the claim that no action is purely for others' benefit and with the reason that all action is based on self-interest. The reason stretches “self-interest” so broadly that it risks explaining every possible choice without distinguishing selfishness from care.

A person who donates time anonymously to help strangers may feel satisfaction afterward. That feeling does not prove satisfaction was the motive or that the strangers' welfare did not matter. People can have mixed motives, and an action can genuinely aim to benefit someone else even if the actor also values acting well.

The opposing argument is strongest when public generosity brings praise or status. A corporation might announce a charity project primarily to improve its reputation. We should examine conduct and consequences rather than assume noble motives from a label. But evidence that some acts serve self-interest does not establish that all do.

There is also a difference between having a reason to act and seeking a personal advantage. A parent may stay awake caring for a sick child because the child's suffering matters to them. Calling that concern self-interest merely because the parent wants the child well empties the term of its ordinary meaning.

Human motives are complex and often intertwined. The claim and reason make a universal assertion they cannot support. We should be willing to identify self-serving acts without denying the possibility of sincere concern for others.

topic: To understand the most important characteristics of a society, one must study its major cities.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the statement and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the statement might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
essay:
Major cities reveal much about a society, but they cannot by themselves show its most important characteristics. I partly disagree with the statement because the experiences of smaller communities and the ties between regions are equally revealing.

A city concentrates government, industry, media, and people from different backgrounds. Studying its housing, transport, and public spaces can show whose needs institutions prioritize. A city's cultural scene may also display how traditions change when groups meet.

Yet a rural district may sustain a language or practice scarcely visible in the capital. The cost of food, the structure of work, and access to schools can differ greatly outside a major city. If a researcher studies only urban residents, the resulting portrait may mistake a large city's opportunities and conflicts for the entire society.

Cities depend on other places for workers, energy, food, and ideas. Following those connections can explain more than treating the city as a self-contained symbol. The same policy may benefit urban consumers while burdening distant producers.

The statement is valuable as an invitation to examine a dense setting where social choices become visible. It is misleading as a complete method. To understand a society, we should compare its cities with other communities and investigate the relationships that bind them.

topic: Educational institutions have a responsibility to dissuade students from pursuing fields of study in which they are unlikely to succeed.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim. In developing and supporting your position, be sure to address the most compelling reasons and/or examples that could be used to challenge your position.
essay:
Schools should give students candid information about the demands of a field, but they should be cautious about dissuading someone from pursuing it. I partly disagree with the recommendation. A prediction of failure can be mistaken, particularly when past performance reflects inadequate preparation rather than a fixed limit on ability.

Suppose a student wants to study physics but struggles with algebra. An advisor who simply says that physics is not for her may close a path she could follow after extra mathematics instruction. A more helpful response would explain the prerequisite, offer tutoring, and set a concrete point at which she can reassess her progress. The institution takes academic standards seriously without treating a present weakness as permanent.

The costs of unqualified encouragement are also real. A nursing program, for instance, has demanding clinical requirements and responsibilities to patients. If a student repeatedly fails essential safety assessments after receiving meaningful support, an advisor should explain the evidence and discuss related careers. Allowing the student to invest additional time and money while concealing serious concerns would not respect her autonomy. The conversation should be based on observed performance and available remedies, not assumptions about background or personality.

The strongest argument for dissuasion arises when a program has clear, necessary standards and the student has enough information to understand the likelihood and costs of continuing. Even then, guidance should preserve choices. A student may choose a slower route, additional preparation, or a different application of the same interest.

Institutions have a duty to advise honestly, provide support, and protect professional standards. They should not become gatekeepers who decide too early which students are destined to succeed. Good advice replaces a vague warning with evidence, options, and an opportunity to improve.

topic: Scandals are useful because they focus our attention on problems in ways that no speaker or reformer ever could.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim. In developing and supporting your position, be sure to address the most compelling reasons and/or examples that could be used to challenge your position.
essay:
Scandals can force hidden problems into public view, but their usefulness depends on evidence and what follows the attention. I partly agree with the statement and reject the suggestion that speakers or reformers can never accomplish the same thing.

A documented corruption case may make an abstract complaint about weak oversight concrete. When records show how officials diverted public funds, citizens can demand an investigation and new safeguards. The event draws attention precisely because it identifies a harm and responsible actors.

Attention alone is unstable. A sensational allegation can harm innocent people if reporting outruns verification. Even a genuine scandal may focus outrage on one person while leaving the system that enabled misconduct intact. Reformers who have studied the problem can explain that system and propose changes after headlines fade. Their work is not replaced by the scandal; it becomes more urgent.

Some problems, such as unsafe workplaces, are addressed through patient organizing before a dramatic incident occurs. Waiting for a scandal would leave people exposed. Public testimony, data, and sustained advocacy can make a problem visible without requiring a catastrophe.

Scandals are useful when they reveal reliable evidence and open a path to accountability. They are not inherently better than reformers. Lasting improvement requires turning a moment of attention into careful investigation and institutional change.

topic: Claim: Governments must ensure that their major cities receive the financial support they need in order to thrive. Reason: It is primarily in cities that a nation's cultural traditions are preserved and generated.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim and the reason on which that claim is based.
essay:
I support adequate funding for major cities, but I do not accept the reason that cities are primarily where a nation's culture is preserved and generated. The claim may be justified by the needs cities serve; the reason overlooks other communities.

A city often provides transit, hospitals, and housing for millions. Underfunding those systems can harm residents and workers throughout a wider region. National or regional support may be appropriate when the city's services benefit people beyond its tax base. Funding decisions should reflect actual needs and transparent results.

Cities also host museums, theaters, and diverse communities that create new forms of art. That supports some cultural funding, but rural towns and smaller communities preserve languages, festivals, and crafts that may later reach urban audiences. Cultural value does not increase automatically with population size. Funding cities on the reason's terms alone could neglect the very traditions displayed in city institutions.

The claim should not become a promise to finance every urban project before basic needs elsewhere are met. Governments must compare the burdens and benefits across regions, including the links among them. A city may thrive because surrounding communities supply food, labor, and ideas.

The reason is at best a partial argument for one aspect of city support. Major cities should receive resources proportionate to the public services they provide and the problems they face, while cultural and economic policy also attends to places beyond them.

topic: Some people believe that government funding of the arts is necessary to ensure that the arts can flourish and be available to all people. Others believe that government funding of the arts threatens the integrity of the arts.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss which view more closely aligns with your own position and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should address both of the views presented.
essay:
I align more closely with the view that public arts funding can help art flourish and remain accessible. The opposing concern is real: a government that pays artists may try to control their messages. Funding should therefore be designed to protect independence.

A small theater may produce work for a local audience but lack wealthy patrons. A public grant can keep tickets affordable and allow young performers to develop. Museums and libraries can similarly bring art to people who could not pay high admission prices. Leaving all support to the market may favor projects with immediate commercial appeal.

The opposing view is strongest when officials select art to reward loyalty or avoid criticism. A grant board that rejects a play because it questions government policy threatens artistic integrity. Transparent criteria, independent reviewers, diverse funding sources, and public reporting can reduce that risk. None eliminates it completely, so artists must remain free to refuse public money.

Private sponsorship can also influence content, even if the pressure is less visible. The issue is not whether funding affects art at all but whether artists have enough independence and varied sources of support to make choices.

I favor public funding because access and experimentation have value beyond ticket sales. It should be allocated through procedures that make political interference difficult and allow audiences and artists to criticize the government that funds it.

topic: Claim: In any field — business, politics, education, government — those in power should step down after five years. Reason: The surest path to success for any enterprise is revitalization through new leadership.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim and the reason on which that claim is based.
essay:
I disagree with the claim that every leader should leave office after five years, and the reason that new leadership is the surest path to success is too simple. Renewal matters, but it can occur through accountability, collaboration, and succession planning as well as replacement.

A company that has grown complacent may benefit when a new director challenges routine assumptions. A political office with weak oversight may need term limits to prevent power from hardening into personal control. These examples give the reason some force.

Yet a school leader may spend several years establishing a curriculum and learning what students need. Removing her automatically just as improvements take effect could disrupt the work. A new leader may bring ideas but also lose institutional memory. The value of change depends on performance and the nature of the project, not a universal deadline.

Long-serving leaders should still be challenged. Independent reviews, open elections or board evaluations, empowered colleagues, and opportunities for younger staff can expose stagnation. Institutions can cultivate new leadership before it is urgently needed.

The reason identifies one route to revitalization, not the surest in every field. Some roles warrant fixed terms; others need flexible tenure with strong checks. A rule based on results and accountability serves enterprises better than identical five-year limits.

topic: In any field of endeavor, it is impossible to make a significant contribution without first being strongly influenced by past achievements within that field.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the statement and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the statement might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
essay:
Past achievements give newcomers methods, questions, and standards against which to test new work. I mostly agree that significant contributions are strongly influenced by earlier work, though “impossible” may be too absolute in fields where independent discovery can occur.

A scientist proposing a new explanation for a disease must know the evidence that existing explanations account for. Otherwise, the proposal may merely repeat an old mistake. A composer who studies earlier forms can use them, challenge them, or deliberately depart from them. In both cases, influence need not mean imitation; it gives the creator a point of departure.

The claim should not become a demand that every contributor follow tradition closely. An outsider may notice a problem insiders have normalized. A child might invent a useful local solution without studying the history of design. Even then, language, tools, and shared practices inherited from others usually shape the work indirectly.

Institutions should therefore teach the history of a field while making room for critical questions. Knowing prior achievements saves time and helps identify a genuine advance. Treating them as untouchable would turn influence into a barrier.

Significant work rarely emerges from a vacuum. Its originality is often clearest when we understand what it builds on and what it changes. The statement captures that relationship, provided it leaves room for unexpected contributors and independent observation.

topic: Nations should pass laws to preserve any remaining wilderness areas in their natural state, even if these areas could be developed for economic gain.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss your views on the policy and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider the possible consequences of implementing the policy and explain how these consequences shape your position.
essay:
I favor legal protection for remaining wilderness even when development promises economic gain, though a compelling public need may justify a narrowly reviewed exception. The danger is that short-term revenue can obscure an irreversible loss.

A forest may protect water supplies, provide habitat, and allow future generations to study an intact ecosystem. A mine might create jobs and tax revenue, but roads and contamination could permanently alter those benefits. Officials should compare the full costs rather than count only the project's immediate output.

The promise of jobs deserves respect, especially in a region with few alternatives. Governments can invest in other industries, compensate affected workers, or consider less damaging sites. Preservation imposed without consulting local communities may be unfair. It may also fail if residents bear all the costs while distant people receive the benefits.

Not every use has the same impact. A carefully located road to an isolated hospital differs from a project whose gains accrue mainly to a private company. Laws can establish protected cores and demand strong evidence, consultation, and mitigation before an exception is considered.

The recommendation is most advantageous where damage cannot be undone and the projected profit is uncertain or narrowly distributed. It is less clear when an urgent, broadly shared need has no feasible alternative. A presumption of preservation, rather than automatic approval of development, properly reflects the stakes.

topic: People's behavior is largely determined by forces not of their own making.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the statement and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the statement might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
essay:
Forces beyond a person's control influence behavior profoundly, but people retain some capacity to choose and change. I partly agree with the statement, while rejecting a deterministic reading that would erase responsibility.

A child whose neighborhood has unsafe streets may play outdoors less than a child with a nearby park. A worker facing unpredictable hours may miss an appointment even when health matters to her. These outcomes cannot be understood fairly without examining the options people actually have.

At the same time, people can respond differently to similar constraints. Neighbors might organize to request a safer crossing, and workers might seek collective changes to scheduling. Such actions do not prove the barriers are imaginary; they show that agency operates within limits. It is easier to act when institutions provide protection and support.

The claim can encourage empathy and better policy by drawing attention to poverty, discrimination, and social expectations. It becomes harmful if it implies that no one is accountable for conduct that injures others. Responsibility should consider available alternatives and the likely effects of a choice.

A useful account of behavior combines circumstances and decisions. Reform can expand real options, while individuals can be encouraged to use the options they have. Neither a story of complete freedom nor one of total determination explains human action well.

topic: Governments should offer a free university education to any student who has been admitted to a university but who cannot afford the tuition.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss your views on the policy and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider the possible consequences of implementing the policy and explain how these consequences shape your position.
essay:
I agree that an admitted student who cannot afford tuition should have access to a free university education, provided admission is fair and the government funds quality as well as fees. The recommendation targets a specific barrier that can waste talent.

A student from a low-income household may meet every academic requirement for a nursing degree but be unable to pay. A grant allows her to train for work the community needs. Without it, university places may go disproportionately to families with money, even when ability is widely distributed.

Tuition is not the only obstacle. Books, transport, and housing can also make enrollment impossible. Governments should design aid around actual costs and make the application straightforward. They should also ensure that institutions have enough teachers and facilities; removing fees while overcrowding classes would provide a promise of access without a sound education.

The policy has costs, and eligibility must be administered fairly. A prosperous student should not claim need by manipulating a form, while a poor student should not face an impossible paperwork burden. Public spending on higher education also should not crowd out essential primary schooling or healthcare.

The recommendation is narrower and more defensible than free tuition for every family. It makes admission meaningful for qualified students who lack resources. Done well, it links opportunity to ability and effort rather than household income.

topic: Claim: In any situation, the best way to persuade other people is to present them with facts and statistics rather than with emotional arguments. Reason: Facts are objective, so they are more persuasive than subjective appeals.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim and the reason on which that claim is based.
essay:
I disagree with the claim that facts and statistics are always the best way to persuade, and the reason that facts are objective does not make them automatically more persuasive than emotion. Good arguments need accurate evidence and an account of why it matters to people.

A city proposing safer crossings should show data on collisions and expected effects of a redesign. Numbers can correct an exaggerated fear and allow residents to compare options. But a parent describing the difficulty of walking a child to school can identify a danger the data failed to measure. The story makes the policy's purpose intelligible; it need not replace the evidence.

Statistics are also selected and interpreted. An average may conceal that a particular neighborhood bears most of the risk. The reason is right that a carefully measured fact can be checked in a way a feeling cannot, but calling every statistical presentation “objective” ignores choices about what to count and how to frame it.

Emotion can mislead when a vivid but unusual case is offered as though it represents everyone. Persuaders should connect personal experience to reliable evidence and acknowledge uncertainty. They should also listen to the audience's values rather than assume a table of figures settles a moral question.

The best method depends on the disagreement. Facts establish what is likely true; emotional understanding can reveal why a consequence matters. Responsible persuasion joins the two instead of declaring one always superior.

topic: Some people believe that success in creative fields, such as painting, fiction writing, and filmmaking, primarily requires hard work and perseverance. Others believe that such success mainly requires innate talents that cannot be learned.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss which view more closely aligns with your own position and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should address both of the views presented.
essay:
I align more closely with the view that success in creative fields depends on hard work and perseverance. Innate abilities can offer an early advantage, but skill develops through practice, criticism, and revision.

A young filmmaker may have a strong sense of visual composition. Completing a film still requires writing, directing actors, editing scenes, and solving problems when a plan fails. Those abilities improve through repeated projects and feedback. A first impression of talent cannot perform that work on the artist's behalf.

The other view captures real differences. Some people begin with unusual sensitivity to rhythm or language, and no amount of effort guarantees the same level of achievement for everyone. Opportunity also matters: a talented painter without materials or time may struggle to develop. We should not describe success as a simple reward for effort while ignoring these conditions.

Yet calling talent unlearnable can discourage beginners before they have had a fair chance to practice. A writer whose early stories are weak may improve dramatically by reading closely and revising. Even an unusually gifted writer needs discipline to turn a promising idea into a finished book.

Hard work is not sufficient for public recognition, which also depends on audiences and luck. It is nevertheless the more useful and generally necessary foundation of creative success. Talent may influence a starting point; perseverance determines how far an artist can develop it.

topic: In business, education, and government, it is always appropriate to remain skeptical of new leaders until those leaders show that they are worthy of trust.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim. In developing and supporting your position, be sure to address the most compelling reasons and/or examples that could be used to challenge your position.
essay:
Skepticism toward a new leader can protect an institution from misplaced trust, but treating distrust as the appropriate default in every setting can prevent cooperation. I partly agree with the statement if skepticism means asking for evidence and accountability, not assuming bad faith.

A new director who promises to improve a struggling school should explain the plan, listen to teachers, and report results. Staff need not believe that every promise will succeed. They can cooperate with a reasonable trial while checking whether the director responds to feedback. Trust grows from conduct, not a title.

Excessive suspicion has costs. If employees refuse to share information until a leader proves complete worthiness, the leader may lack the knowledge needed to act well. Citizens face a similar problem when they treat every new official as dishonest before examining a decision. A leader deserves a fair opportunity to demonstrate judgment.

The stakes and powers of the role matter. An official controlling public funds should face strong oversight from the outset, regardless of personal reputation. Clear procedures can protect everyone without making every interaction hostile. Skepticism should focus on claims and safeguards rather than on a presumption of guilt.

Trust is best built through transparent decisions, consistent behavior, and a willingness to correct errors. New leaders should earn deeper confidence over time. Institutions can remain open to their ideas while maintaining checks from the first day.

topic: Claim: Group assignments that students must work together to complete should replace a substantial amount of traditional lecture-based instruction in college and university courses. Reason: It is vital for students to gain experience collaborating with peers to study a topic and to achieve a common goal.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim and the reason on which that claim is based.
essay:
I agree that group assignments should form a substantial part of some university courses, and the reason is persuasive: students need experience working with peers toward a common goal. I disagree that they should broadly replace lectures without regard to subject or design.

In an engineering course, a team can build a prototype and discover how difficult it is to coordinate decisions, divide tasks, and test a shared result. Each student may need to explain a design choice and respond to a teammate's criticism. Those skills are difficult to learn from listening alone.

The reason does not show that a lecture is obsolete. A concise explanation of a difficult concept can give students a common foundation before they work together. A poorly managed group project may allow one student to do most of the work while others receive the same grade. Instructors should set individual responsibilities and evaluate both collaboration and understanding.

The right balance depends on the aim. A seminar may use discussion and joint research extensively, while a course introducing technical foundations may need direct instruction followed by practice. Students should learn to collaborate, but also to think independently and master material they cannot delegate.

The claim captures a real weakness in passive instruction. Its reason supports well-designed group work, not an indiscriminate substitution. Universities should combine explanation, individual work, and collaboration in proportions that serve the learning goal.

topic: Universities should require every student to take a variety of courses outside the student's field of study.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim. In developing and supporting your position, be sure to address the most compelling reasons and/or examples that could be used to challenge your position.
essay:
Courses beyond a major can give university students tools they would not encounter in a narrow program. I support requiring some breadth, provided the requirement leaves room for depth and does not become an inflexible checklist.

An engineering student who studies public policy may recognize that a technically efficient water system can fail if residents cannot afford access. A literature student who takes statistics may better evaluate claims about reading habits or social inequality. In both cases, the second discipline changes how the student uses the first. Universities have reason to introduce connections students might not seek on their own.

Yet extra courses have costs in tuition and time. A student already balancing work with a demanding degree might be delayed by a large set of unrelated requirements. The institution should offer meaningful choices, transfer credit where appropriate, and design courses that invite serious engagement. It should not confuse collecting credits with becoming educated.

Breadth is particularly advantageous when it complements specialization and creates informed citizens. It is less advantageous when a rigid rule prevents a student from completing essential training or imposes avoidable debt. A modest, thoughtfully chosen requirement serves the recommendation better than an indiscriminate one.

topic: A nation should require all of its students to study the same national curriculum until they enter college.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss your views on the policy and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider the possible consequences of implementing the policy and explain how these consequences shape your position.
essay:
A common national curriculum can guarantee access to important knowledge, but requiring every student to study exactly the same material until college would ignore local needs and individual development. I partly disagree with the statement.

Shared instruction in literacy, mathematics, science, and civic history can protect students whose schools might otherwise offer a thin education. A family moving between regions should not find that a child has missed an essential prerequisite. Common standards also give the public a basis for asking whether schools serve students fairly.

Uniformity becomes harmful when it prescribes every text, project, and pace. A coastal community may use local ecology to teach scientific methods; another may study water scarcity. Both can meet the same underlying standard. Students who need additional language support or advanced work may require different routes to mastery. A rigid curriculum could force teachers to move on before one group understands or leave another unchallenged.

National content can also become a political instrument if one authority decides that only a single interpretation of history may be taught. Opportunities to compare sources and question claims are part of a sound civic education.

A better policy establishes a core of knowledge and skills, then gives schools room to adapt examples, offer electives, and support different learners. Equal educational opportunity requires shared expectations, but it does not require identical lessons for every child.

topic: Educational institutions should actively encourage their students to choose fields of study that will prepare them for lucrative careers.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim. In developing and supporting your position, be sure to address the most compelling reasons and/or examples that could be used to challenge your position.
essay:
Colleges should help students understand lucrative career paths, but they should not steer every student toward them as though salary were the main purpose of education. I partly disagree with the statement.

A student from a low-income family may benefit from learning which qualifications lead to stable, well-paid work. Clear information about costs, salaries, and internships can expand choices that the student did not know existed. Avoiding the subject of earnings in the name of intellectual freedom could leave some graduates with debt they cannot manage.

Yet salary alone does not predict a good match. A student who excels at teaching and wants to work with children may find sustained purpose there even if another field pays more. Pushing her into an occupation she dislikes could lead to poor work and eventual departure. Labor markets also change during the years a degree takes to complete.

An institution should disclose outcomes honestly and allow students to explore interests through courses and practical experience. It can show how a field connects to several careers and help students develop transferable skills. This is guidance, not an instruction to maximize income.

Lucrative work is a legitimate goal, especially when financial security is urgent. Educational institutions serve students best when they help each person weigh that goal against aptitude, purpose, debt, and the realities of the profession.

topic: Some people believe that in order to be effective, political leaders must yield to public opinion and abandon principle for the sake of compromise. Others believe that the most essential quality of an effective leader is the ability to remain consistently committed to particular principles and objectives.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss which view more closely aligns with your own position and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should address both of the views presented.
essay:
I align more closely with the view that effective political leaders need stable principles, though they must be willing to compromise on methods. The opposing view recognizes the need to respond to public opinion, but yielding to every demand can leave a leader without a coherent purpose.

A mayor committed to accessible transport might alter the location of a bus stop after residents explain that the planned site is unsafe. That change respects public evidence while preserving the objective. By contrast, abandoning the entire project whenever a poll moves would make long-term planning impossible.

Principles can also become an excuse for refusing to listen. A leader who insists that an original plan is perfect may ignore people whom it harms. Political responsibility includes explaining a goal, examining objections, and revising means when the facts warrant it. Compromise is not necessarily surrender.

The first view is strongest when public opinion reveals an overlooked need or when a policy cannot be implemented without broad support. The second is strongest when a temporary majority asks a leader to violate rights or discard a well-supported long-term commitment. Judgment is needed to distinguish these cases.

I prefer principled leadership because it gives citizens a basis for evaluating decisions across time. Good leaders neither chase every poll nor treat criticism as disloyalty. They hold their central commitments openly and adapt their plans to serve those commitments better.

topic: Formal education tends to restrain our minds and spirits rather than set them free.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the statement and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the statement might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
essay:
Formal education can restrain curiosity when it rewards only obedience, but I disagree that it generally holds minds and spirits back. A well-designed education supplies the knowledge and habits that make independent thought possible.

A student who learns how to examine historical sources gains more freedom to question a familiar story. A science class that asks students to test competing explanations can make them less dependent on a confident authority. Structure and instruction are not opposites of freedom; they can provide tools for exercising it.

The criticism has force in a school that treats a single memorized answer as the end of every discussion. Rigid tracking may discourage a child from attempting a difficult subject. Institutions can also privilege one culture's perspective while leaving others unheard. These failures are reasons to reform teaching and assessment.

Unstructured freedom is not enough on its own. A student without access to books, feedback, or expert guidance may never encounter ideas beyond the immediate environment. Good teachers introduce unfamiliar material, set demanding standards, and invite learners to argue with reasons.

Education should be judged by what students can do after leaving: read critically, revise beliefs, create, and keep learning. It can fail that test, but its best practices expand rather than confine the mind.

topic: The well-being of a society is enhanced when many of its people question authority.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the statement and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the statement might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
essay:
A society benefits when many people question authority, provided the questions are informed and directed toward accountability rather than mere reflexive distrust. I mostly agree with the statement.

Residents who ask why a city contract was awarded to a particular company may uncover favoritism or simply obtain a clear explanation of the decision. Either outcome improves public understanding. Workers who challenge an unsafe procedure can prevent harm before it becomes a scandal. Institutions are more reliable when those affected can speak without fear.

Questioning is not the same as rejecting every expert conclusion. During a disease outbreak, citizens should ask how a recommendation was tested and what uncertainty remains. They should also be willing to accept strong evidence. An endless demand for impossible certainty could obstruct a useful response.

Authorities need room to act, especially in emergencies. Clear roles and procedures can make quick action possible while preserving later review. A culture of questions should reward careful reasons and correction, not treat every disagreement as a contest of status.

The well-being of a society rests partly on the ability of ordinary people to expose mistakes and propose better ways to act. Questioning authority is valuable when it strengthens evidence, rights, and accountability. It becomes harmful when suspicion is prized more than learning the answer.

topic: Governments should focus on solving the immediate problems of today rather than on trying to solve the anticipated problems of the future.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the recommendation and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, describe specific circumstances in which adopting the recommendation would or would not be advantageous and explain how these examples shape your position.
essay:
Governments must address urgent problems, but focusing on the present instead of anticipated future harms is a false economy. I disagree with the recommendation as a general rule, while accepting that immediate suffering can demand priority.

If a city has residents without safe drinking water, it should not delay repairs to fund a speculative long-term project. The need is concrete and severe. Yet maintaining flood defenses before a predicted storm is also a response to present evidence. Waiting until homes are underwater would increase both human and financial costs.

Many future problems develop slowly. Investment in education, disease surveillance, and infrastructure may not produce a dramatic result this year, but neglect can make later crises harder to solve. Officials should compare the likelihood and severity of a risk with the cost of prevention. They need not fund every imagined danger equally.

The recommendation is most persuasive when future forecasts are uncertain and current needs are unmet. It is least persuasive when a foreseeable, preventable threat is treated as someone else's problem merely because its full effects lie ahead. Public budgets can reserve resources for both immediate relief and measured prevention.

Good government does not choose one time horizon once and for all. It protects people facing harm now while taking proportionate action to prevent serious harm to those who will live with today's decisions.

topic: Some people believe that college students should consider only their own talents and interests when choosing a field of study. Others believe that college students should base their choice of a field of study on the availability of jobs in that field.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss which view more closely aligns with your own position and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should address both of the views presented.
essay:
I reject both extremes in the choice between personal interests and available jobs. I lean toward the view that students should begin with their talents and interests, while treating employment information as an important constraint.

A student who enjoys statistics may work hard enough to master difficult methods and discover applications in health, finance, or public policy. That motivation is valuable. Choosing a field solely because vacancies are currently plentiful could lead another student into work she cannot sustain. Labor markets can also shift before graduation.

The job-focused view has a serious point for students who face debt or need to support family. A college should publish costs and outcomes, arrange practical experience, and help students compare routes into work. Encouraging a passion without a credible plan for earning a living would not respect the student's circumstances.

The interest-focused view also needs qualification. What a student already knows and enjoys at eighteen is not the limit of future ability. Courses and internships can reveal an unfamiliar field that fits both aptitude and opportunity. Choice should be exploratory rather than a single calculation made from either a salary table or a childhood hobby.

I favor a process that starts with curiosity and ability, tests them against real work, and uses employment evidence to design a viable path. Students need room to pursue meaningful study and honest information about its costs and possibilities.

topic: Laws should be flexible enough to take account of various circumstances, times, and places.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the statement and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should consider ways in which the statement might or might not hold true and explain how these considerations shape your position.
essay:
Laws should be flexible enough to account for circumstances, but flexibility must be structured so that similar people receive similar treatment. I agree with the statement when it calls for proportionate judgment rather than unlimited discretion.

A fixed penalty for every missed filing deadline might punish a person hospitalized unexpectedly as severely as someone who repeatedly ignores the rule. Allowing an appeal with clear evidence can preserve the purpose of the law without imposing needless hardship. Likewise, building standards may need to reflect different climates while protecting the same level of safety.

Too much flexibility can create unfairness. If officials can waive requirements whenever they like, people with influence may receive exceptions denied to others. The law should state its aims, define relevant factors, require written reasons, and permit review. Those safeguards make adaptation accountable.

Some principles should not bend with local custom. Equal protection and basic procedural rights must apply across places and times, even when the practical rules used to enforce them vary. Flexibility is valuable in means and remedies, not as an excuse to abandon a core commitment.

The best laws combine a stable purpose with procedures that consider real differences among cases. Mechanical uniformity can be unjust, but discretion without standards can be just as harmful.

topic: Claim: The best way to understand the character of a society is to examine the character of the men and women that the society chooses as its heroes or its role models. Reason: Heroes and role models reveal a society's highest ideals.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim and the reason on which that claim is based.
essay:
A society's heroes can reveal ideals it wants to celebrate, so I partly agree with the claim and reason. They do not, however, provide the best complete account of its character, because public praise may differ from ordinary conduct.

When schools commemorate a civil rights advocate, the choice suggests that equality and courage are valued. Debates over a monument can reveal competing understandings of the past. In that sense the reason is sound: role models offer evidence about stated ideals.

But the claim makes a stronger inference than the reason supports. A nation may honor a champion of fairness while maintaining institutions that exclude some citizens. Official heroes may reflect the preferences of powerful groups, while other communities admire people whose names never appear on monuments. To understand character, we need to compare ideals with behavior, laws, and opportunity.

Heroes may also be chosen for different qualities by different generations. That change is informative, but it prevents a single list from standing for a whole society. A researcher should ask who selected the role models, who disagreed, and whether the ideals shaped daily life.

The reason supports studying heroes as one valuable source. It does not establish that they are the best source by themselves. A society's character emerges in the gap between the virtues it praises and the practices it actually sustains.

topic: Some people believe that it is helpful to view a challenging situation as an opportunity for personal growth. Others believe that reimagining challenging situations this way occupies too much of the focus one needs to face challenges effectively.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss which view more closely aligns with your own position and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should address both of the views presented.
essay:
I lean toward the view that seeing a challenge as an opportunity for growth can help people respond, but the opposing view rightly warns against turning that attitude into a distraction from concrete action.

A student who fails an exam may feel less defeated if she treats the result as information about her study method. She can review errors, seek help, and practice differently. The growth frame is useful because it encourages a next step rather than a judgment that she is incapable.

The same frame can be harmful if it demands that every difficulty feel inspiring. Someone facing eviction needs information about legal aid, income, and housing, not a lecture about personal development. Optimistic language can also shift attention away from an institution that caused avoidable harm. A person may learn from the experience and still insist that the harm should not have occurred.

The two views address different parts of the response. Interpretation can influence motivation, while action addresses the external problem. The student should make a study plan; the tenant should seek practical support. Reflection is most useful after urgent needs are met or alongside them, not as a substitute.

I favor the growth perspective as a voluntary tool, not a moral duty imposed on people in crisis. Its worth depends on whether it helps someone see choices and take effective action.

topic: Some people believe that traveling to and living in numerous places increases one's ability to relate and connect to other people. Others believe that this ability is better cultivated by living in one place and developing a deep understanding of that community.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss which view more closely aligns with your own position and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should address both of the views presented.
essay:
I lean toward the view that living in different places can help people connect across backgrounds, though deep roots in one community can teach a different and equally important form of understanding.

A person who has lived in several countries may learn that familiar gestures or assumptions do not carry the same meaning everywhere. Navigating language and customs can make the person more willing to ask questions rather than presume. These experiences can help in a diverse workplace or neighborhood.

The second view points to a limit of travel. Brief stays may produce a collection of impressions rather than lasting relationships. Someone who remains in one place and spends years working with neighbors through disputes, illness, and change may understand human needs more deeply than a frequent traveler. Stability can teach patience and accountability.

Neither mobility nor rootedness automatically produces empathy. A traveler can remain insulated in familiar circles; a lifelong resident can be curious about newcomers. The decisive habits are listening, humility, and continued contact with people whose experiences differ from one's own.

I prefer the first view as a source of broad perspective, but it should be paired with the depth emphasized by the second. Moving widely expands the range of encounters; staying and investing in relationships reveals how much an initial encounter leaves unknown.

topic: Claim: Young people's tendency to make extensive use of portable devices like smartphones and tablets has hurt their development of social skills. Reason: These devices encourage users to form artificial personalities and relationships online rather than fully and honestly engaging with the people around them.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim and the reason on which that claim is based.
essay:
I partly agree that extensive device use can weaken some young people's social practice, but I reject the reason's broad claim that online relationships are inherently artificial or dishonest. The effects depend on what young people do online and what opportunities they retain offline.

A teenager who spends every gathering checking messages may miss chances to read facial expressions, negotiate disagreements, and pay attention to friends in the room. Those are skills learned through practice. Parents and schools can create device-free spaces and model conversation without treating all digital contact as a problem.

Online communities can also support honest relationships. A student who feels isolated at school may find peers with a shared interest and speak openly in a way that was difficult locally. Maintaining such friendships can involve empathy, patience, and conflict resolution. A profile may be selective, but face-to-face social life also involves self-presentation.

The reason is strongest when platforms reward a polished persona and constant comparison. Young users may hide uncertainty to win approval. Media literacy and supportive offline relationships can help them recognize that pressure. Simply banning devices would not teach them how to communicate well in an increasingly digital world.

The claim identifies a risk, not an inevitable developmental outcome. Young people need varied practice: attentive face-to-face interaction and thoughtful use of digital spaces. Neither medium guarantees honesty, and neither makes it impossible.

topic: Claim: When one is making a decision, it is better to have a limited number of options. Reason: The more options a person has, the more difficult it is to make a rational decision.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim and the reason on which that claim is based.
essay:
I partly agree that a limited set of meaningful options can make decisions easier, but I disagree that fewer options are always better. The reason identifies a cognitive burden; it does not account for the value of having a suitable choice available.

A patient comparing dozens of nearly identical insurance plans may struggle to understand differences. Presenting a short list that meets the patient's needs, with clear information about cost and coverage, can improve the decision. Removing irrelevant complexity helps reason rather than restricting it.
