But a university that offers only two fields of study might force a student into a poor fit. More options can expand freedom and allow people to match their abilities to opportunities. The problem arises when alternatives are numerous, poorly explained, or incomparable, not from choice itself.

Decision makers can use criteria before looking at options. A student may first decide which subjects, costs, and career possibilities matter, then narrow a broad list. Advisers can organize choices without eliminating them. In high-stakes decisions, time and reliable information may matter more than the raw count.

The reason supports structuring choices and reducing trivial variations. It does not prove that a limited number is intrinsically more rational. A good decision requires enough genuine alternatives to meet different needs and a practical way to compare them.

topic: Because people increasingly feel compelled to share their personal details online, the right to privacy is eroding.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the claim. In developing and supporting your position, be sure to address the most compelling reasons and/or examples that could be used to challenge your position.
essay:
The right to privacy faces new pressure as people share personal details online, but sharing is not always voluntary or informed. I largely agree that privacy is eroding, while rejecting the idea that individual oversharing is the only cause.

A person may post a photograph for friends without realizing that it reveals a location or can be copied beyond the intended audience. Even someone who rarely posts may have information collected by applications, employers, or data brokers. The boundary between a chosen disclosure and extensive tracking is easy to miss.

Online sharing also has benefits. People can maintain relationships, organize community work, and seek support for sensitive problems. A demand that everyone simply withdraw from digital life would place the burden of protection on users while leaving powerful collectors of data unchanged.

Privacy can be strengthened through clear consent, limited retention, secure defaults, and rules that let people access or delete information about themselves. Users should also think carefully about an audience and future consequences before posting. Both institutional design and individual habits matter.

The claim captures a real trend in the loss of control over personal information. The right itself need not disappear. It requires stronger protections suited to a world in which data can be copied, combined, and inferred long after a person first shared it.

topic: Some people believe that journalism should make news entertaining to keep the public engaged and informed. Others believe that this practice prioritizes entertainment and undermines the mission of journalism.
instructions: Write a response in which you discuss which view more closely aligns with your own position and explain your reasoning for the position you take. In developing and supporting your position, you should address both of the views presented.
essay:
I align more closely with the view that making news entertaining can undermine journalism, although clear storytelling can help people pay attention to important facts. The crucial distinction is whether entertainment serves reporting or becomes its measure of success.

A reporter covering a complex housing policy can use a resident's experience, a clear graphic, and concise language to make the issue understandable. Those choices engage an audience without changing the evidence. Journalism should not demand that people endure confusing presentation to receive reliable information.

The opposing risk appears when a newsroom selects only dramatic conflicts or treats every policy discussion as a contest of personalities. A surprising clip may attract viewers while leaving out the budget figures or context needed to judge a claim. If attention is the main reward, a slow but consequential investigation may receive less support than a sensational rumor.

Audiences do need reasons to follow the news. An accurate story with no structure may fail to inform simply because readers abandon it. Editors can test whether engaging elements illuminate the subject, identify uncertainty, and preserve proportion. They should correct errors even when a false version would draw more clicks.

I favor journalism's mission of verification over entertainment as an aim. Compelling presentation is valuable when it carries careful reporting to more people. It becomes destructive when facts are selected or distorted merely to keep an audience watching.
